meta.title: Core Scientific (CORZ): Adam Sullivan's Post-Bankruptcy Reinvention — From North America's Largest Bitcoin Miner to AI Infrastructure Landlord, the $8.7 Billion CoreWeave Anchor, and the Race to Deploy 1.5 Gigawatts of High-Performance Computing Capacity Across the American South
meta.abstract:
Core Scientific, Inc. (Nasdaq: CORZ) entered 2024 as one of the most dramatic restructuring stories in the brief history of publicly traded bitcoin mining. Having filed for Chapter 11 in December 2022 under the weight of collapsed bitcoin prices, surging energy costs, and a leveraged SPAC balance sheet, the Austin, Texas-based company emerged from bankruptcy in January 2024 with a clean capital structure and a leadership team — led by CEO Adam Sullivan, a former XMS Capital digital-asset banker installed mid-crisis in 2023 — already executing a strategic pivot that would prove far more consequential than its origins in the proof-of-work economy.

The pivot is structural, not cosmetic. Core Scientific owns or controls approximately 724 megawatts of operational data center capacity across five states, purpose-built for the extreme power density and thermal demands of bitcoin mining — infrastructure that translates, with selective retrofitting, into highly competitive colocation assets for AI and high-performance compute (HPC) workloads. Sullivan's insight, crystallized in a landmark June 2024 agreement with GPU cloud provider CoreWeave, was that the company's owned real estate, existing grid interconnections, and operational expertise in managing dense electrical loads were scarcer and more durable than the bitcoin mining margins they had historically supported.

The CoreWeave contract — initially 200 megawatts at an estimated $3.5 billion over twelve years, subsequently expanded through successive option exercises to approximately 390 megawatts and $8.7 billion in cumulative contracted revenue — established Core Scientific as the anchor AI infrastructure landlord for one of the fastest-growing GPU cloud operators globally. By Q1 2026, 243 megawatts were actively billing, adjusted EBITDA turned positive for the first time in the transition era, and a $3.3 billion project bond priced at 7.75% — one of the largest single infrastructure debt raises in the sector that year — funded construction reserves across six conversion sites.

The dossier examines three interlocking narratives: the operational transformation from self-mining to colocation and the unit economics that make 80–85% gross margins achievable at scale; the capital structure journey from a $400 million convertible note offering through the mega project bond and toward a projected $2 billion capital deployment in 2026 alone; and the corporate governance evolution following the failed CoreWeave acquisition attempt (July–October 2025), an activist campaign by Two Seas Capital, and a board reconstitution that added former Equinix CEO Steve Smith as a strategic anchor voice. Frozen snapshot date: 2026-05-23.

chapters.title: The Landlord of the AI Boom: Core Scientific's Strategic Position at the Snapshot Date
chapters.body:
As of May 23, 2026, Core Scientific is billing 243 megawatts of high-performance computing capacity to CoreWeave across its converted data center sites, collecting revenue at a quarterly run rate that already exceeds its entire 2025 colocation haul. The $3.3 billion project bond, priced in April at 7.75%, has settled into the capital structure. Adjusted EBITDA has turned positive for the first time in the HPC transition era. The company that filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in December 2022 with approximately $1.4 billion in assets and a shattered balance sheet now carries an $8 billion market capitalization and a contractual revenue backlog of $8.7 billion stretching twelve years into the future.

## An Accidental Infrastructure Giant

The strategic thesis is deceptively simple, and it begins with an observation that Adam Sullivan articulated to investors repeatedly in the months following his arrival as President in May 2023: bitcoin mining, for all its reputational wreckage, had been the world's most demanding stress-test of the operational and engineering requirements that now define frontier AI data center construction. High-density power delivery, continuous thermal management, large-scale electrical infrastructure in power-rich but logistics-challenged markets — the discipline of running one of North America's largest mining fleets had forged exactly the capabilities that hyperscalers and GPU cloud operators needed from a colocation landlord but rarely found.

Sullivan's insight was that Core Scientific did not need to become something new. It needed to redirect what it already was. The company owned the real estate, held the grid interconnections, and had proven it could manage the extreme power densities that NVIDIA's latest GPU generations demanded. What it lacked, in early 2024, was a tenant willing to underwrite the conversion economics at scale. CoreWeave provided that underwriting — and the June 2024 anchor contract transformed the thesis from aspiration into executable strategy.

## Three Narratives, One Company

The full story of Core Scientific's reinvention unfolds across three distinct arcs, each carrying its own logic and its own risk.

The first is **operational conversion**: the physical transformation of bitcoin mining facilities across Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, North Carolina, Texas, and Oklahoma into GPU-dense AI data centers under long-term colocation contracts. The work is capital-intensive — $279.2 million in capital expenditure in FY2025 alone, with $2 billion guided for 2026 — and technically demanding. Each site conversion requires custom power infrastructure, cooling systems engineered for GPU thermal loads, and the construction management discipline to deliver capacity on the schedules that CoreWeave's own customer commitments require.

The second is **capital structure evolution**: the arc from a balance sheet that collapsed under $400 million of equipment-lender and convertible-note debt in 2022 to the project finance architecture that the $3.3 billion bond represents. That bond — described by industry observers as one of the largest single infrastructure debt raises in the AI sector — was underwritten against the cash flows of CoreWeave's twelve-year fixed-price contracts, validating the proposition that colocation revenue from a creditworthy AI tenant is bankable infrastructure collateral.

The third is **governance**: the contested corporate independence question that erupted when CoreWeave proposed an all-stock acquisition in July 2025, was rejected by shareholders at a roughly 10-to-1 ratio in October, and culminated in the February 2026 cooperation agreement with activist investor Two Seas Capital that reconstituted the board and installed former Equinix chief executive Steve Smith as a director.

## The Financial Foundation

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Contracted CoreWeave revenue | $8.7 billion (12-year terms) |
| MW billing at snapshot | 243 MW |
| Q1 2026 colocation revenue | $77.5 million |
| Q1 2026 Adjusted EBITDA | +$4.4 million |
| HPC gross margin guidance | 80–85% |
| Market capitalization | ~$8 billion |
| 2026 guided capex | ~$2 billion |

The Q1 2026 colocation revenue figure is instructive in isolation: $77.5 million in a single quarter from 243 megawatts, against $65.4 million from colocation across all of FY2025. With 450-plus megawatts targeted by late summer 2026 and 590 megawatts by early 2027, the revenue inflection is not a projection — it is already visible in the reported numbers.

Core Scientific stands furthest advanced among bitcoin-mining-origin companies in the AI infrastructure pivot; Riot Platforms and Marathon Digital remain earlier-stage comps with limited contracted HPC revenue, while Equinix, trading at approximately 20 times forward EBITDA, represents the aspirational peer multiple that Core Scientific's valuation re-rating would require.

What the snapshot cannot resolve are the execution risks that the following chapters will examine in detail: whether construction pace across nine active sites and two greenfield pipelines can meet contracted delivery schedules; whether customer concentration in a single tenant — CoreWeave — represents a structural vulnerability or a durable anchor; and whether the layered capital structure of project bonds, convertible notes, and warrant liabilities can absorb the unexpected without triggering the kind of balance-sheet event that ended the company's first chapter in December 2022.

chapters.title: Proof of Work: From a Seattle Startup to SPAC Excess, Bankruptcy, and Rebirth
chapters.body:
## Seattle Beginnings

Core Scientific was incorporated on December 13, 2017, in Seattle, Washington, by Darin Feinstein and Michael Jeffrey Levitt at a moment when bitcoin's first great retail mania was cresting toward its peak. The founders' premise was straightforward: that the industrial-scale extraction of proof-of-work rewards would require professional infrastructure operators, not basements and self-assembled rigs. They positioned the company as an enterprise-grade digital asset mining and blockchain infrastructure operator, and in December 2018 raised approximately $50 million in a seed round — substantial capital for a sector that most institutional allocators still regarded as speculative theater.

Kevin Turner, a former Microsoft chief operating officer with deep enterprise technology credentials, joined as chief executive officer in 2018, lending the nascent company the kind of management legitimacy required to attract larger checks. Under Turner's tenure, Core Scientific extended its fundraising arc with a $44 million Series A in early 2020 and a $21 million debt round in May of that year, bringing total pre-SPAC capital to roughly $115 million. Turner departed in May 2021, just as the company was preparing the transaction that would define — and nearly destroy — it.

## The SPAC Moment

By late 2021, the blank-check vehicle boom had reached its apex, and mining companies with tangible assets and credible growth narratives were among the most sought-after targets. On January 20, 2022, Core Scientific completed a reverse merger with Power & Digital Infrastructure Acquisition Corp., trading under the ticker XPDI, in a transaction that assigned the combined entity an implied valuation of approximately $4.3 billion and delivered net cash proceeds of roughly $195 million to Core Scientific's balance sheet. BlackRock served as the XPDI anchor investor, a detail that lent the transaction an institutional imprimatur it would not long retain.

The timing was nearly perfectly catastrophic. Core Scientific closed the SPAC merger at what proved to be almost the precise peak of the bitcoin market cycle. The transaction structure loaded the balance sheet with equipment financing obligations — loans secured against the company's ASIC mining hardware — and convertible note liabilities that had been issued in anticipation of the cash flow a rising bitcoin price would generate. When bitcoin began its prolonged descent, those obligations did not adjust.

## The Collapse

The arithmetic of 2022 was brutal and compounding. Bitcoin fell from above $47,000 at the start of the year to below $17,000 by December. Electricity costs, already the dominant variable in mining economics, surged alongside broader energy markets. The equipment loans, priced against hardware valuations that had since collapsed, continued to accrue. Core Scientific had also taken on hosting customers — third-party miners leasing rack space — whose contracts had been structured in ways that, under some circumstances, caused the company to absorb power cost increases that would ordinarily have been passed through.

By midsummer 2022, the company had begun sending warning signals to creditors. By autumn, management was in active negotiations over the terms of a restructuring. On December 21, 2022, Core Scientific filed for Chapter 11 protection in the Southern District of Texas, Case No. 22-90341, reporting assets of approximately $1.4 billion and liabilities of approximately $1.3 billion. The company engaged Weil, Gotshal & Manges as restructuring counsel, PJT Partners as investment banker, and AlixPartners as financial adviser — a canonical creditor-rights advisory roster that signaled a managed rather than chaotic insolvency. DIP financing was arranged to sustain operations during the proceeding.

Feinstein and Levitt, the founders who had built the company from a Seattle seed round, receded from the operational picture. Neither would remain in an executive or board role in the reorganized entity.

## The Recruiter's Hire

The board's most consequential decision during the Chapter 11 proceeding was not a legal maneuver but a hiring one. In May 2023, roughly five months into the reorganization, Core Scientific recruited Adam Sullivan as president. Sullivan was thirty-two years old and had spent the preceding six years at XMS Capital Partners, a Chicago-based middle-market investment bank that specialized in digital asset and infrastructure M&A transactions, where he served as managing director and head of digital assets and infrastructure, overseeing more than $5 billion in cryptocurrency mining deal flow.

Sullivan was, in effect, the antithesis of the founders: not a technologist or a bitcoin idealist, but a transaction engineer who had spent years pricing, structuring, and financing the infrastructure underlying the mining industry. He understood what the assets were worth in alternative use cases, and he arrived with a thesis already formed. He was elevated to chief executive officer in August 2023, roughly six months before the company would emerge from bankruptcy. His CFO, James Nygaard, followed from XMS Capital, where Nygaard had served as managing director and head of M&A.

Sullivan's pitch to creditors, distilled: the company's real assets were not the bitcoin miners but the real estate, the grid interconnections, and the operational expertise that had been built around managing extreme electrical loads. Those assets, he argued, were acutely scarce against the backdrop of an accelerating demand surge for artificial intelligence compute infrastructure. Converting the same power-dense facilities from proof-of-work mining to GPU colocation would generate higher revenues, more durable margins, and a dramatically different investor-relations story.

## Emergence and Relisting

The restructuring plan was confirmed on January 16, 2024, by the bankruptcy court. The reorganization eliminated approximately $400 million in equipment-lender and convertible-note debt through conversion to equity — a standard creditor-to-owner reorganization mechanism — and left the company with a substantially delevered balance sheet. On January 24, 2024, Core Scientific relisted on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker CORZ. The founders' names appeared nowhere in the leadership filings.

The company that emerged was, in meaningful respects, a different legal and operational entity from the one that had filed fourteen months earlier. The ownership structure had been reconstituted around creditors-turned-shareholders. The strategic direction had been reoriented by a CEO who had been hired specifically to execute a pivot that the pre-bankruptcy management had never contemplated. The bitcoin mining equipment remained operational — cash flow from self-mining would fund the transition — but it was now explicitly a depreciating asset to be harvested, not a growth platform to be expanded.

## The Proof Point

The first public evidence that Sullivan's thesis was executable arrived on June 3, 2024, less than five months after the Nasdaq relisting, when Core Scientific announced a 200-megawatt, twelve-year HPC colocation agreement with CoreWeave, the NVIDIA-backed GPU cloud operator that had become the dominant infrastructure layer for large-scale AI model training and inference. The estimated cumulative revenue: $3.5 billion over the contract term.

The announcement was received by analysts as a structural rerating event. What had been priced as a distressed mining company was now presenting a landlord-model revenue stream with the characteristics of infrastructure debt: long-dated, fixed-price, and backed by a counterparty with access to the capital markets. CoreWeave subsequently exercised contract options in rapid succession — an additional approximately 70 megawatts on June 25, 2024, adding $1.225 billion in projected revenue; a final tranche of approximately 120 megawatts on October 22, 2024, adding $2.0 billion more. A further $1.2 billion expansion at the Denton, Texas site was announced in February 2025. The cumulative contracted relationship reached approximately 390 megawatts and $8.7 billion over twelve years.

## Two Companies in One Ticker

The corporate history of Core Scientific is, in effect, the story of two separate companies that happen to share a name, a set of physical assets, and a stock exchange listing. The first company — the Seattle startup that raised venture capital, went public through a SPAC at a $4.3 billion valuation at the peak of a bitcoin cycle, and filed for bankruptcy when the market turned — was built by founders who believed in the perpetual economics of proof-of-work mining. That company no longer exists in any meaningful organizational sense: its founders are gone, its equity was extinguished, and its strategic logic was repudiated by its own failure.

The second company — the one led by Adam Sullivan, anchored by an $8.7 billion CoreWeave contract, and financed in April 2026 by a $3.3 billion project bond — was assembled from the wreckage by a transaction specialist who looked at the physical infrastructure and saw something the miners had never built it to be: a piece of AI data center real estate. The chapters that follow examine how that reinvention was executed, what it cost, and whether the company can sustain it at the scale its development pipeline now demands.

chapters.title: Megawatts as Product: Data Center Platforms, Conversion Architecture, and the HPC Colocation Stack
chapters.body:
## A Three-Segment Architecture in Motion

Core Scientific organized its operations into three formal reporting segments: HPC/AI Colocation, Digital Asset Self-Mining, and Digital Asset Hosted Mining. The taxonomy was sequential in both strategic and temporal terms — the company was executing a deliberate migration from the latter two into the first, and the pace of that migration defined the entire investment thesis.

The segment boundaries, however, obscured a deeper technical reality: the infrastructure underpinning all three was fundamentally the same. Bitcoin mining at industrial scale is, at its core, an exercise in managing extreme power density and dissipating extraordinary amounts of heat. ASIC mining hardware drew between 20 and 30 kilowatts per rack — power densities that required robust three-phase electrical distribution, precision airflow or liquid cooling, reliable fiber connectivity, and physical security infrastructure. These were precisely the prerequisites for deploying dense NVIDIA GPU clusters for AI training and inference workloads. The distinction was not one of infrastructure type but of compute payload — and that convergence was the architectural foundation of the conversion strategy.

## The Site Portfolio: Nine Facilities, Five States

As of the May 2026 snapshot, Core Scientific operated approximately 724 megawatts of owned data center capacity across nine sites: Auburn, Alabama; two facilities in Dalton, Georgia; Lexington, Kentucky; Marble, North Carolina; Williston, North Dakota; and the Denton, Texas Polaris campus. The geographic distribution was deliberate — these markets had been selected over years for access to relatively low-cost grid power, available land, and favorable permitting environments. They also sat within utility service territories that had built significant generation capacity for industrial loads that had since declined, leaving interconnection capacity available at costs and lead times that would be unachievable in coastal markets competing directly for hyperscaler demand.

The development pipeline extended considerably further. At Pecos, Texas, Core Scientific held development rights for a site with a stated long-term leasable capacity target of 1.5 gigawatts — a project that, if fully realized, would constitute one of the largest single AI data center developments in North America. In Hunt County, Texas, an announcement in 2026 identified approximately 430 megawatts of gross development capacity. At Port Muskogee in Oklahoma, Phase 1 construction was underway for 100 megawatts, with a long-term pipeline of 1.5 gigawatts disclosed. Together, the Pecos and Muskogee pipelines represented a potential total development target of three gigawatts — a figure requiring years of grid coordination and capital deployment to realize, but one that underscored the ambition of the company's land and interconnection position.

Power procurement and grid interconnection status varied by site, reflecting different stages of the conversion program. The Polaris campus had the most advanced HPC-readiness profile, with substantial conversion already completed and active billing to CoreWeave underway. At sites earlier in the conversion sequence, interconnection upgrade work — involving new substation capacity, switchgear, and metering infrastructure calibrated for data center loads rather than mining loads — formed a significant component of each site's capital program.

## The Conversion Architecture: From ASIC to GPU

The physical conversion of a bitcoin mining facility to GPU colocation was neither trivial nor equivalent in cost to greenfield construction — and the delta between those two figures was the structural source of Core Scientific's competitive position.

A bitcoin mining deployment configured its power distribution to feed rows of ASIC rigs drawing uniform, predictable loads. GPU cluster deployments for AI workloads required reconfigured power distribution units, upgraded circuit breakers, and precision power conditioning accommodating the variable draw profiles of dense GPU nodes. The transition also demanded cooling infrastructure modifications: ASIC facilities used high-volume air circulation designed around the thermal signature of mining rigs, while AI GPU deployments — particularly for the liquid-cooled NVIDIA H100 and H200 generations — required direct liquid cooling loops, rear-door heat exchangers, or chilled-water plant upgrades. Fiber and networking infrastructure represented an additional conversion layer, with upgrades to dense fiber plant, redundant carrier interconnects, and meet-me-room capacity required by GPU cloud operators. Physical security systems also required enhancement, as AI data center clients imposed cage-level isolation, multi-factor access, and 24/7 staffing standards that exceeded typical mining facility protocols.

The aggregate per-megawatt conversion capital expenditure was substantially below greenfield development cost. A new AI data center in a power-constrained market might require $10 to $15 million per megawatt in total development cost — inclusive of land, civil works, utility interconnection, and fit-out. Core Scientific's conversion program leveraged existing buildings, existing grid interconnections, and existing thermal infrastructure, compressing that figure materially. The company received approximately $226.2 million in CoreWeave partnership reimbursements in [FY2025](https://investors.corescientific.com/financial-information/sec-filings), partially offsetting its $279.2 million in capital expenditure for the year — a structure reflecting the shared economics of converting existing assets for a specific tenant's benefit.

## Polaris: The Proof-of-Concept at Hyperscale

The Polaris campus at Denton, Texas, functioned as the flagship demonstration of the conversion model. The original CoreWeave anchor contract announced in June 2024 encompassed multiple Core Scientific sites, but Polaris represented the largest single-site concentration of the partnership. In February 2025, Core Scientific announced a further $1.2 billion incremental expansion of the CoreWeave relationship at the Denton site — a commitment that elevated Polaris into a different category of infrastructure project.

By the Q1 2026 reporting period, construction at Polaris was progressing toward the 450-plus-megawatt billing milestone targeted for late summer 2026. The site was already contributing to the 243 megawatts of active billing that generated $77.5 million in colocation revenue in the first quarter — an annualized colocation run rate of approximately $310 million that management characterized as the business's inflection point. The April 2026 $3.3 billion project bond, secured against CoreWeave contract cash flows across six sites, treated the Polaris contracted revenue as among the anchors validating the project finance structure to institutional fixed-income investors.

The significance of Polaris extended beyond megawatt count. It demonstrated that the conversion model could be executed at hyperscale pace — hundreds of megawatts of operational HPC colocation built within roughly eighteen months of a contract announcement, a speed that greenfield developers could not match given utility interconnection lead times routinely extending three to five years. For potential additional HPC tenants evaluating Core Scientific's capabilities, Polaris functioned as a reference deployment that no pure-play data center developer could replicate from a standing start.

## Self-Mining: The Managed Wind-Down

Digital Asset Self-Mining contributed $229.2 million in revenue in FY2025 — the company's largest single revenue segment — a figure that illustrated both the scale of Core Scientific's legacy mining operation and the magnitude of the displacement underway. The self-mining fleet comprised multiple ASIC hardware generations, with the company's aggregate hashrate representing a meaningful share of the Bitcoin network's total computational output.

Management stated publicly the intention to consolidate self-mining to one or two sites by the end of 2026. The sequencing of this wind-down was a critical operational challenge: converting a site from mining to colocation required taking megawatts offline for conversion work, interrupting mining revenue without immediately replacing it with colocation billing. The ramp-up of CoreWeave billing — structured in tranches as converted megawatts came online — was designed to close that gap, but the transition had created a trough in blended revenue that FY2025 exemplified, with total company revenue declining 37.5% to $319.0 million from $510.7 million in FY2024.

The revenue mix inversion was already beginning to accelerate. The $65.4 million in total colocation revenue recorded across all of FY2025 gave way to $77.5 million in a single Q1 2026 quarter. As the self-mining footprint contracted toward one or two sites and colocation capacity scaled toward 500-plus megawatts, a business that generated roughly 72% of its FY2025 revenue from mining was on trajectory to generate the majority from colocation before year-end 2026.

## Operational Engineering: PUE, Uptime, and the Data Center Management Layer

The conversion from bitcoin mining to GPU colocation was not merely a physical transformation — it was an operational one. Running ASIC mining equipment tolerated variation in temperature, humidity, and power quality within ranges that would be unacceptable for AI workloads running on NVIDIA GPU clusters, where a hardware fault in a training run could destroy days of accumulated computation.

Core Scientific's colocation contracts with CoreWeave were structured around uptime commitments approaching the 99.99% availability standard typical of hyperscale-grade data center agreements. Achieving and sustaining that standard required investment in redundant power paths — N+1 or 2N UPS configurations — redundant cooling plant, and 24/7 network operations center coverage with defined escalation procedures. Power usage effectiveness, the ratio of total facility power draw to IT load power draw, was both an efficiency metric and a commercial imperative: lower PUE translated to lower energy cost per unit of compute, improving margins within the fixed-price contract structure. Operators targeting hyperscaler tenants typically committed to PUE figures below 1.4, with best-in-class facilities at or below 1.2.

The accumulated operational know-how — built over years of managing extreme power density, maintaining thermal tolerances, and running 24/7 infrastructure across geographically distributed facilities — represented intellectual capital not easily replicated by new entrants. It was the operational substrate beneath the contractual and financial architecture of the CoreWeave relationship, and the reason Core Scientific's management framed the HPC pivot not as a departure from its core competency but as its fullest expression: the same discipline that kept ASIC mining rigs running at 98% uptime in the Alabama summer was the discipline required to guarantee a GPU cluster operator the availability windows on which its enterprise customers depended.

chapters.title: Trough, Inflection, and Ramp: Revenue Trajectory, Margin Architecture, and Capital Structure
chapters.body:
## The Trough

The single number that defines Core Scientific's financial narrative through FY2025 is $319.0 million — the total revenue the company reported for the year ending December 31, 2025, down 37.5 percent from the $510.7 million recorded in FY2024. Presented without context, that decline reads as corporate deterioration. Presented correctly, it is the deepest point of a deliberately engineered trough: the financial signature of a company that was destroying one business and building another, and had not yet reached the quarter where the new business generated enough revenue to compensate for what was being retired.

The FY2025 segment breakdown tells the story in granular terms. Self-mining contributed $229.2 million, still the dominant revenue line but one management had explicitly scheduled for reduction. Hosted mining — infrastructure leased to third-party bitcoin operators — added $24.4 million, a category in active wind-down as those megawatts convert to higher-margin uses. HPC/AI colocation, the future of the enterprise, produced just $65.4 million for the full year, reflecting the lag between capital deployment and revenue recognition. Construction begins, conversion capital is spent, megawatts come online — but colocation revenue accrues only once a tenant begins billing. That sequencing, standard in project finance, meant FY2025 gross profit was just $37.9 million on $319.0 million of revenue, a blended gross margin of approximately 11.9 percent. That figure, stripped of context, would suggest a commoditized, capital-intensive business with minimal pricing power. It suggests nothing of the sort.

## The Inflection

The Q1 2026 earnings release, filed in May 2026, made the transition legible in a single data point: colocation revenue of $77.5 million in one quarter, against $65.4 million in all twelve months of FY2025. With 243 megawatts billing as of March 31, 2026 — up from the nascent deployments that produced FY2025's colocation line — the annualized run rate from colocation alone had reached approximately $310 million, a figure that already exceeds total FY2025 company revenue before a single additional megawatt comes online.

Total Q1 2026 revenue reached $115.2 million. Adjusted EBITDA turned positive for the first time in the HPC transition era, reaching $4.4 million. Management characterized the quarter as the inflection point the company had been constructing toward since the CoreWeave anchor deal closed in June 2024.

> "We are at the inflection point," Adam Sullivan said on the Q1 2026 earnings call. "243 megawatts are billing, and we are on track to 450-plus megawatts by late summer."

## The Forward Revenue Trajectory

The mathematical logic of the CoreWeave contract — $8.7 billion over twelve years across approximately 390 contracted megawatts — implies an annualized steady-state colocation revenue of roughly $725 million per year once fully billed. That figure represents roughly a 4.7x multiple of the company's entire FY2025 colocation revenue, to be achieved through contract ramp-up rather than new customer acquisition.

The milestones that govern the ramp are sequential: 450-plus megawatts targeted by late summer 2026, 590 megawatts by early 2027. At 590 megawatts of billing, applying the implied per-megawatt economics of the CoreWeave contracts, colocation revenue alone approaches $1.1 billion on an annualized basis. Combined with residual self-mining revenue — consolidated to one or two sites by year-end 2026 per management guidance — total company revenue at that milestone likely exceeds $1.2 billion, more than tripling FY2025 levels within roughly two years of the trough.

| Scenario | Colocation MW Billing | Est. Annual Colocation Revenue | Est. Mining Revenue | Total Revenue Estimate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2026 Annualized | 243 MW | ~$310M | ~$200M | ~$510M |
| Late Summer 2026 | 450 MW | ~$575M | ~$150M | ~$725M |
| Early 2027 | 590 MW | ~$755M | ~$80M | ~$835M |
| Long-term (1 GW) | 1,000 MW | ~$1.28B | ~$30M | ~$1.31B |

## Margin Architecture

The 11.9 percent blended gross margin of FY2025 is perhaps the most misleading figure on Core Scientific's income statement. It reflects a business in which the dominant revenue contributor — self-mining at $229.2 million — carries gross margins broadly in line with bitcoin mining economics: volatile, energy-cost-sensitive, capital-intensive. Colocation, by contrast, operates on fundamentally different unit economics: once conversion capital is deployed and a tenant begins billing, the incremental cost of delivering power and maintaining the facility is a small fraction of the contract price.

Management initially guided colocation gross margins at 75–80 percent. In Q1 2026, that guidance was raised to 80–85 percent, reflecting favorable cost performance as the first clusters reached operational steady state. At the 82.5 percent midpoint, the gross profit contribution per megawatt-year approaches levels that no mining business — at any bitcoin price — can match.

The blended company-wide margin at various billing scales illustrates the transformation underway:

| MW Billing | Colocation Revenue | Colocation Gross Profit (82.5%) | Mining Revenue | Mining Gross Profit (~25%) | Blended Gross Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 243 MW | $310M | $256M | $200M | $50M | ~62% |
| 450 MW | $575M | $474M | $150M | $38M | ~70% |
| 590 MW | $755M | $623M | $80M | $20M | ~78% |
| 1,000 MW | $1,280M | $1,056M | $30M | $8M | ~82% |

The trajectory confirms that blended company gross margins are approaching data center territory — 70–80 percent and rising — as mining revenue fades from the mix. Consensus FY2027 Adjusted EBITDA estimates in the range of $600–800 million reflect that margin expansion assumption.

## The Capital Structure: Three Layers

Core Scientific's balance sheet, as of December 31, 2025, and restructured further by the April 2026 project bond, operates across three distinct financial layers, each with different risk, cost, and equity-dilution characteristics.

**Layer one: the $3.3 billion project bond.** Priced in April 2026 at 7.75 percent, due 2031, senior secured against the cash flows from CoreWeave's long-term colocation contracts, the bond generated net proceeds of approximately $2.9 billion after issuance costs and reserve funding. The proceeds repaid existing debt and capitalized construction reserves across six CoreWeave sites. Industry observers described it as one of the largest single infrastructure debt raises in the AI sector in 2026. The transaction's significance extends beyond its size: by accepting the CoreWeave contracts as project finance collateral, lenders effectively certified that the twelve-year fixed-price agreements are bankable at scale — a validation of the underlying contract structure that no amount of management commentary could replicate.

**Layer two: the $1.06 billion convertible notes.** Issued in August 2024, these 3.00 percent senior unsecured notes mature September 1, 2029, with a conversion rate of approximately 90.93 shares per $1,000 principal. At current share prices, the notes function as equity-adjacent instruments: holders willing to convert capture exposure to CORZ upside, while the 3.00 percent cash coupon is modest relative to market rates, reflecting the embedded equity option. The $1.06 billion face value represents a manageable obligation given the project bond proceeds and the forward EBITDA trajectory, but the 2029 maturity concentrates refinancing risk in a window before the project bond matures.

**Layer three: warrant liabilities.** The $936.1 million fair value of outstanding warrants — CORZW and CORZZ tranches issued as part of the Chapter 11 reorganization — creates the most volatile element of Core Scientific's reported financials. These liabilities are marked to market each quarter, and because warrant value is a function of the underlying share price, volatility in CORZ stock (five-year beta of 5.45) produces enormous non-cash swings in reported earnings with no relationship to operating performance.

## The Non-Cash Noise Problem

Nothing illustrates the inadequacy of GAAP net income as a performance metric for Core Scientific more vividly than two consecutive quarters: Q4 2025 and Q1 2026.

In Q4 2025, the company reported net income of $216 million — a figure that sounds like a breakthrough. The dominant driver was a $330.3 million non-cash gain from the revaluation of warrant liabilities as CORZ shares declined during the period. Remove that mark-to-market reversal and the quarter was barely profitable on an operating basis.

In Q1 2026 — the quarter management itself called the inflection point — the company reported a net loss of $347.2 million. That loss was driven by a $266.5 million non-cash goodwill and long-lived asset impairment charge and a $30.8 million non-cash warrant and CVR revaluation. Strip those items and the quarter was, for the first time in the transition era, generating positive Adjusted EBITDA of $4.4 million on a rapidly improving revenue mix.

The implication for investors is clear: GAAP net income at Core Scientific is an unreliable signal. Adjusted EBITDA — which excludes depreciation, amortization, stock-based compensation, non-cash impairments, and warrant fair value changes — is the correct operating lens. Analysts covering the name have universally adopted this framing, and the company's own investor communications lead with Adjusted EBITDA and operating cash flow metrics.

## Capital Deployment

FY2025 capital expenditure of $279.2 million was partially offset by $226.2 million in CoreWeave partnership reimbursements — a structural feature of the colocation model in which the anchor tenant contributes toward conversion capital, dramatically reducing Core Scientific's net cash outlay to equip the facilities. That reimbursement dynamic means the company's capital efficiency on the first tranches of CoreWeave buildout is substantially better than gross CapEx figures suggest.

FY2026 guidance of approximately $2 billion in capital expenditure — including roughly $700 million for the Hunt County, Texas site acquisition and the Polaris/Muskogee purchase — represents a step-change in deployment pace funded primarily by the $2.9 billion in project bond net proceeds. Free cash flow will be negative through the construction phase; that is expected and does not represent financial deterioration. It represents the conversion of bond proceeds into contracted revenue-generating infrastructure, a sequence as standard in project finance as it is counterintuitive when viewed through a traditional equity earnings lens.

## Peer Benchmarking and the Re-Rating Trade

At approximately $8 billion market capitalization as of the snapshot date, Core Scientific trades at roughly 25 times consensus 2026 Adjusted EBITDA — a multiple that sits between the mining-company peer group and the data center operator peer group, reflecting exactly the market's uncertainty about which bucket to apply.

| Company | Business | Market Cap | EV/EBITDA Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core Scientific (CORZ) | Mining-to-AI pivot (advanced) | ~$8B | ~25x 2026E |
| Equinix (EQIX) | Mature data center REIT | ~$70B+ | ~20x |
| Riot Platforms (RIOT) | Mining-to-AI pivot (early stage) | ~$4–5B | 8–10x |
| Marathon Digital (MARA) | Primarily BTC treasury + mining | ~$5–6B | 6–8x |

The re-rating trade thesis is mechanical: as colocation revenue reaches 70–80 percent of the total revenue mix — a milestone visible by late 2026 on current ramp trajectories — the logical peer group shifts from Riot and Marathon toward Equinix and Digital Realty. A data center multiple of 18–22 times applied to consensus FY2027 EBITDA of $600–800 million implies an equity value meaningfully above current prices, even accounting for the net debt introduced by the project bond. Whether the market grants that re-rating incrementally, as each MW billing milestone is achieved, or in a larger step-function as the revenue mix decisively crosses a threshold, is the central question for equity holders in the near term. The financial architecture, at least, has been constructed to make the answer legible: each quarter's colocation revenue figure is a progress report on the transformation, and the numbers are now moving fast enough that ambiguity has a short shelf life.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
The central question confronting any analyst approaching Core Scientific's valuation as of late May 2026 was which comparables to apply. The company was shedding a mining identity but had not yet fully earned a data center one. That ambiguity — frozen mid-transformation — was precisely what made the stock both treacherous and interesting.

## A Stock Re-rating in Real Time

At the frozen snapshot of May 23, 2026, Core Scientific carried an approximate market capitalization of $8 billion, derived from a share price trading within a fifty-two-week range of $10.46 to $26.83 against a beta of 5.45 — numbers that together described a security as volatile as any liquid large-cap on the Nasdaq. The implied enterprise value, layering in the [$3.3 billion project bonds](https://investors.corescientific.com/news-releases/news-release-details/core-scientific-reports-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) at 7.75 percent due 2031 and the $1.06 billion in convertible notes at 3.00 percent due 2029, and subtracting $533.4 million in cash and digital assets carried at year-end 2025, placed the enterprise value in the vicinity of $11.8 billion. Against trailing FY2025 total revenue of $319 million — a trough-year figure that dramatically understated forward earnings power — the trailing EV/Sales multiple of roughly 37 times was economically meaningless as a standalone measure. The market was not pricing what Core Scientific had earned. It was pricing what it was becoming.

## Forward Multiples and the Earnings Inflection

The more instructive frame was prospective. Core Scientific entered 2026 with 243 megawatts billing under the CoreWeave contracts, generating $77.5 million in colocation revenue in the first quarter alone — an annualized run rate of approximately $310 million from that segment in isolation. With 450-plus megawatts targeted by late summer 2026 and 590 megawatts by early 2027, an extrapolation of the Q1 2026 revenue rate across an average of roughly 350 megawatts billing for the full year suggested a plausible FY2026 colocation revenue figure in the range of $400 to $460 million, supplemented by declining but still material self-mining contributions. Total FY2026 revenue on that basis could approach $580 to $650 million — roughly double the FY2025 reported trough.

Management, on the Q1 2026 earnings call, characterized the quarter as "the inflection point in the mining-to-AI conversion," and the financial arithmetic supported the description: Q1 2026 marked the first positive Adjusted EBITDA in the transition era, at $4.4 million, with colocation gross margins guided to the 80 to 85 percent range — raised from the original 75 to 80 percent guide — as the CoreWeave sites approached operational maturity.

The [consensus estimate for FY2027 Adjusted EBITDA](https://investors.corescientific.com/financial-information/sec-filings), as reflected in sell-side coverage tracked against the snapshot date, clustered in the $600 million to $800 million range. Against the $11.8 billion enterprise value, that produced a forward EV/EBITDA range of approximately 14.8 times to 19.7 times on FY2027 estimates — a multiple that straddled the boundary between the mining-company peer group and the data center operator peer group. On a forward price-to-sales basis against the annualizing colocation run-rate, the valuation began to look more defensible: at $8 billion of equity value against $400 to $460 million of FY2026E colocation revenue, the colocation segment alone implied a multiple in the 17 to 20 times range — high for an infrastructure company, but not unreasonable if the 80-plus percent gross margins were sustainable at scale and the CoreWeave contracts proved bankable for their full twelve-year tenor.

## Peer-Group Comparison

The complexity of constructing a peer table for Core Scientific was the absence of a pure-play analog. No other listed company as of late May 2026 had executed the same mining-to-AI-colocation conversion at comparable scale. The relevant comparisons sat at the two poles of Core Scientific's potential identity.

| Company | Ticker | Approx. Market Cap | Fwd. EV/EBITDA | Business Mix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Core Scientific | CORZ | ~$8.0B | ~15–20x (FY27E) | Mining-to-AI pivot; 390 MW contracted |
| Equinix | EQIX | ~$75B | ~21–23x | Data center REIT; global hyperscale colocation |
| Digital Realty | DLR | ~$48B | ~19–21x | Data center REIT; wholesale and retail colo |
| Riot Platforms | RIOT | ~$4–5B | NM / elevated | Bitcoin mining; early-stage AI pivot |
| Marathon Digital | MARA | ~$5–6B | NM / elevated | Bitcoin treasury + mining; minimal AI pivot |
| Iris Energy | IREN | ~$1–2B | NM / elevated | AI/HPC colocation pivot; smaller scale |

*Peer multiples are approximate estimates derived from publicly available market-cap data and consensus estimates as of the snapshot date. CORZ multiples based on the $11.8 billion enterprise value described above.*

The data center REITs — Equinix and Digital Realty — traded in the 19 to 23 times forward EV/EBITDA range, reflecting the market's willingness to pay a premium for long-duration, predictable, investment-grade-contracted infrastructure cash flows. Core Scientific's CoreWeave contracts shared structural characteristics with those businesses — long tenors, a creditworthy counterparty, fixed or near-fixed pricing — but the company's capital structure complexity, bitcoin mining residual, customer concentration, and equity-market volatility meant it had not yet earned a commensurate multiple. The bitcoin mining peers — Riot and Marathon — commanded no meaningful EBITDA multiple at all, as their earnings remained hostage to bitcoin price fluctuations. Core Scientific's EV/EBITDA range, sitting in the upper reaches of what a pivot-stage miner commanded and the lower reaches of what a pure-play data center operator warranted, mathematically described the market's pricing of the transition itself: something between 40 and 60 percent of the re-rating journey completed.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Price Implied

A scenario-based frame, working from the contracted revenue backlog, illuminated the gap between current pricing and intrinsic value under different execution assumptions. The [CoreWeave contracts](https://investors.corescientific.com/news-releases/news-release-details/core-scientific-reports-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) represented approximately $8.7 billion in nominal cumulative revenue over twelve years — roughly $725 million annually at full 390-megawatt billing. Discounted at a rate appropriate for a BB-rated infrastructure operator carrying project finance debt — call it 9 to 11 percent, with the 7.75 percent coupon on the project bonds as a cost-of-debt anchor — the present value of the contracted stream alone, before any terminal value or expansion optionality, fell in the range of $4.5 billion to $6 billion. The $8 billion equity value, set against approximately $3.8 billion in net debt and implying a total enterprise claim of $11.8 billion, was therefore assigning material value to uncontracted expansion capacity at Pecos, Muskogee, Hunt County, and whatever additional HPC tenant relationships the company could execute beyond CoreWeave.

That expansion optionality was real but binary: it materialized only if Core Scientific could sign additional anchor tenants at comparable economics, execute the greenfield development pipelines at the guided cost, and maintain access to capital markets at reasonable rates. The April 2026 project bond, priced at 7.75 percent, suggested the market believed the contracted cash flows were bankable — but at a spread implying a significant ongoing execution risk premium above a pure data center credit.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case.** Core Scientific signed one or more additional HPC anchor tenants — Microsoft and Google were the most-cited candidates in analyst commentary, though neither relationship was publicly confirmed at the snapshot date — at economics comparable to the CoreWeave relationship, validating the expansion pipelines at Pecos and Muskogee. Self-mining wound down cleanly by late 2026. FY2027 Adjusted EBITDA reached or exceeded $800 million as 590 megawatts billed at full run-rate. The market re-rated the stock toward Equinix-comparable multiples of 20 to 22 times forward EV/EBITDA, implying an enterprise value of $16 to $17.6 billion. After deducting approximately $3.8 billion in net debt, equity value could have approached $12 to $14 billion — a share price in the range of $25 to $30, consistent with or above the fifty-two-week high.

**Base case.** The CoreWeave contracts executed on schedule, 590 megawatts billed by early 2027, and FY2027 Adjusted EBITDA landed at the consensus midpoint of approximately $700 million. No additional anchor tenant was contracted before year-end 2026. The market maintained a blended multiple of 15 to 16 times — crediting the data center transition but discounting customer concentration and capital structure complexity. Enterprise value in the range of $10.5 to $11.2 billion, less net debt, implied equity value of $6.7 to $7.4 billion: broadly consistent with the prevailing market capitalization, suggesting the base case was approximately what the stock was already pricing at the snapshot date.

**Bear case.** Construction delays pushed 590-megawatt billing into 2028. Bitcoin prices declined materially, impairing the residual self-mining economics still funding a portion of corporate overhead. A second HPC anchor tenant failed to materialize, limiting Core Scientific to a single-customer concentration that institutional investors increasingly discounted. FY2027 Adjusted EBITDA printed at $450 to $500 million. A re-rating toward the upper band of the mining-company peer multiple — 9 to 10 times — produced an enterprise value of $4 to $5 billion, approaching or breaching the level of net debt and implying significant equity dilution risk. Share price could have retreated toward or below the fifty-two-week low.

## What the Market Was Pricing

At an $8 billion equity valuation in late May 2026, the market was pricing something between the base and bull cases with a non-trivial tail assigned to the bear. It was crediting the CoreWeave contracts as real, crediting management's operational capability as demonstrated by the Q1 2026 EBITDA inflection and the $3.3 billion project bond execution, but applying a meaningful discount to any value beyond the contracted revenue stream. The gap between the consensus read and the dossier's assessment was narrow on the base case but material on the bull: if Core Scientific could demonstrate a second anchor tenant relationship and begin billing at 590 megawatts without a construction miss, the re-rating from a blended mining/data center multiple toward something approaching pure data center valuation implied 50 to 75 percent upside from the snapshot equity value. The path there ran through execution — permits, power interconnections, and counterparty diversification — and through time. The market, in pricing CORZ at roughly 16 times forward EBITDA in May 2026, was demanding proof before granting the full data center multiple. Adam Sullivan's task, heading into the second half of 2026, was to deliver it.

chapters.title: Quarter by Quarter: Management Commentary, Guidance Cadence, and the Colocation Ramp
chapters.body:
## The First Chapters After Emergence

Core Scientific re-entered public markets on January 24, 2024, less than a week after its Chapter 11 restructuring plan was confirmed. The inaugural post-emergence quarters carried the fingerprints of a business still oriented around bitcoin: FY2024 total revenue reached $510.7 million, a figure that flattered the top line while masking the strategic irrelevance of the underlying revenue composition. Self-mining and hosted mining remained dominant. The CoreWeave anchor agreement had been signed in June 2024, and management was quick to frame the relationship as transformative — but in the first quarters after listing, investors were still largely reading a bitcoin miner's income statement. Colocation revenue was negligible for most of the year, with conversion capital expenditure flowing out while contract revenue had yet to flow in.

The quarterly earnings calls from mid-2024 onward established the rhetorical framework that Adam Sullivan and CFO James Nygaard would sustain through every subsequent release: the megawatt. Not revenue, not earnings, but megawatts billing. The logic was deliberate. Revenue recognition on a long-term colocation contract is a trailing indicator — it follows construction completion, customer acceptance, and the final commissioning of GPU clusters that weigh several tonnes and arrive in shipping containers on unpredictable schedules. Guiding on megawatts allowed management to provide a forward-looking operational signal that investors could verify in real time against announced site conversions, while insulating guidance from the conversion timing uncertainty inherent in any construction-dependent revenue ramp.

## FY2025: The Paradox of the Trough Year

The full measure of the transition's disruption appeared in the FY2025 annual report. Total revenue fell to $319.0 million — a 37.5 percent decline from FY2024's $510.7 million — a number that, taken in isolation, would ordinarily signal a company in distress. The reality was the opposite: Core Scientific was deliberately dismantling its higher-volume, lower-margin mining revenue base and replacing it with lower-volume, substantially higher-margin colocation contracts that were still in build-out.

The segment breakdown told the story clearly. Self-mining contributed $229.2 million, still the largest single segment. Colocation added $65.4 million. Hosted mining contributed $24.4 million. Total gross profit was $37.9 million on $319.0 million in revenue — a blended margin of 11.9 percent — weighed down by the legacy economics of bitcoin mining and by conversion capital expenditure flowing through the income statement. Adjusted EBITDA remained negative across the year. Capital expenditure reached $279.2 million, partially offset by $226.2 million in CoreWeave partnership reimbursements, the accounting expression of a customer effectively co-investing in its own supply chain.

The quarterly cadence through FY2025 was a study in the gap between financial statements and operational progress. Each quarter, Sullivan and Nygaard updated the megawatt count — the number of contracted megawatts actively billing CoreWeave — as the primary indicator of business health. The trajectory pointed upward; the reported financials pointed downward. That divergence, and management's insistence that investors focus on the former rather than the latter, required a level of investor confidence in the strategic thesis that the CoreWeave anchor contract's $8.7 billion in contracted revenue helped provide.

## The Megawatt Guide: Revenue Math at Each Milestone

The precision with which management articulated the MW-to-revenue conversion made the megawatt guide more than a construction progress metric — it was an implicit revenue forecast. At full billing on 243 megawatts, Q1 2026 colocation revenue of $77.5 million implied an annualized run rate of approximately $310 million from colocation alone, already exceeding all of FY2025's colocation revenue by a factor of 4.7 in a single quarter.

| MW Milestone | Approximate Annualised Colocation Revenue | Status (as of snapshot) |
|---|---|---|
| 243 MW (Q1 2026 actual) | ~$310M | Billing |
| 450+ MW (late summer 2026 target) | ~$570M | Under construction |
| 590 MW (early 2027 target) | ~$745M | Contracted |

At 590 megawatts — the contractually committed endpoint of the initial CoreWeave build-out — annualised colocation revenue at current per-MW rates would approach or exceed $745 million, well above FY2025 total company revenue of $319 million. The gross margin guided to 80–85 percent on those contracts meant that by the time 590 megawatts was fully billing, colocation gross profit alone would likely exceed Core Scientific's total revenue from any prior year of its existence.

Management guided on megawatts rather than dollars for a second structural reason: the 80–85 percent gross margin guidance (raised in Q1 2026 from the original 75–80 percent guide, a 500-basis-point lift attributed to construction cost efficiencies and contract optimisation) meant that investors could independently compute the earnings implications from the MW count without management exposing itself to quarterly revenue recognition timing risk that it could not fully control.

## Restatement: A Footnote With Implications

Embedded in the FY2024 financials was a disclosure that attracted auditor scrutiny and investor attention in equal measure: a restatement related to the improper capitalisation of demolition-related asset values during the mining-to-colocation facility conversion. The restatement carried no impact on revenue, Adjusted EBITDA, or cash flows — management and auditors were explicit on that characterisation — but it reflected the accounting complexity inherent in a business that was simultaneously demolishing one set of assets and constructing another within the same physical facilities. Converting a bitcoin mining shed into a GPU colocation hall requires stripping out mining hardware, upgrading cooling infrastructure, installing new electrical distribution, and often reinforcing floors and rooflines for the weight of GPU racks. The boundary between costs properly expensed as demolition and costs properly capitalised as new construction was not always obvious, and the restatement confirmed that the initial judgements had erred toward capitalisation. The correction tightened that accounting treatment without altering the economic story.

## The Acquisition That Wasn't: Earnings Call Messaging Through the CoreWeave Bid

No external event disrupted the earnings cadence more abruptly than CoreWeave's all-stock acquisition offer, announced July 7, 2025. The proposal offered Core Scientific shareholders a fixed exchange ratio of CoreWeave shares — a structure that immediately drew shareholder opposition given CoreWeave's own post-IPO valuation uncertainty and the implicit subordination of Core Scientific's contracted cash flows to CoreWeave's equity multiple. Management walked a narrow line through the summer and early autumn 2025 earnings calls: it could not advocate publicly against a deal its board had agreed to, but it was also obligated to disclose the shareholder pressure building against the transaction.

The October 30, 2025 shareholder vote produced one of the more decisive rejections in recent infrastructure M&A: approximately 203.5 million shares voted against, 20.8 million in favour, and 21.6 million abstained — a roughly ten-to-one rejection. The commercial CoreWeave colocation contracts were explicitly unaffected by the termination. When management spoke to investors in the subsequent earnings call, the strategic repositioning was swift and direct: independence was characterised not as a consolation prize but as a strategic asset. Core Scientific, the messaging held, was now free to pursue additional HPC tenant relationships — analysts had cited Microsoft and Google as potential counterparties — without the conflicts of interest that a CoreWeave ownership structure would have created.

## Q1 2026: The Inflection Point

The Q1 2026 earnings release, published in May 2026, delivered the data point management had been forecasting toward for six quarters: Adjusted EBITDA turned positive, reaching $4.4 million on $115.2 million in total revenue, with colocation contributing $77.5 million as 243 megawatts billed. Sullivan characterised the quarter as the inflection point in the mining-to-AI conversion — the moment at which the colocation ramp had grown large enough relative to the legacy mining base that the consolidated economics began to reflect the higher-margin business rather than the lower-margin one being wound down.

Bitcoin price sensitivity remained a material consideration even in this milestone quarter. Self-mining still contributed a substantial share of total revenue, and management acknowledged that a 10–20 percent move in bitcoin prices affects reported earnings materially — a $22 to $46 million revenue swing on the $229.2 million FY2025 self-mining base, before operating cost effects. The company's stated intention to consolidate self-mining to one or two sites by end-2026 would progressively reduce that exposure, but in Q1 2026 the bitcoin price remained a meaningful variable in the quarterly financial model.

The gross margin guidance raise — to 80–85 percent from 75–80 percent — provided CFO Nygaard's clearest forward signal on the colocation trajectory. At those margins, each additional 100 megawatts of billing adds roughly $35–40 million in gross profit annually at current per-MW economics, implying that the step from 243 to 450-plus megawatts carries approximately $70–80 million in incremental annual gross profit, with the further step to 590 megawatts adding another $50–60 million. The arithmetic of the ramp — and the company's insistence on measuring it in megawatts — had, by Q1 2026, finally aligned with reported financial results convincingly enough that the inflection characterisation was difficult to dispute.

chapters.title: The Bankers Who Built a Data Center Company: Sullivan, Nygaard, and the Board Reconstitution
chapters.body:
## The Banker Who Became an Operator

Adam Sullivan was thirty years old and eight months into a new job when the company that had recruited him filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. He had joined Core Scientific as President in May 2023 — the company was already deeply distressed, its stock suspended, its creditor negotiations grinding forward in the Southern District of Texas — and by August of that year he held the chief executive title as well. By the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, he was thirty-three, overseeing a Nasdaq-listed infrastructure company with an $8 billion market capitalization, $3.3 billion in freshly priced project bonds, and a twelve-year contractual relationship with CoreWeave worth a nominal $8.7 billion. The biographical arc is unusual enough to merit examination: what kind of person gets recruited to lead an insolvent company at thirty, and what does that background reveal about how the company was subsequently run?

Sullivan's credentials were not operational. He held a B.S. in Financial Economics from the University of Rochester, spent two years as a quantitative analyst at M&T Bank, moved to the buy side as an analyst at Indian Wells Capital Management, and then spent nearly six years at XMS Capital Partners, a Chicago-based middle-market investment bank specializing in digital assets and infrastructure. At XMS, he rose to Managing Director and Head of Digital Assets and Infrastructure, where he oversaw more than $5 billion in cryptocurrency mining transactions — a period that made him arguably the most deeply transactionally networked person in the institutional bitcoin mining sector. He knew the equipment lenders, the power brokers, the site developers, and the M&A advisors. He had seen the capital structure of every significant mining company at the moment of maximum financial stress. When Core Scientific's restructuring advisors went looking for someone who could execute a pivot from mining to high-performance computing while simultaneously managing creditor negotiations, they found a 30-year-old banker who had modeled versions of exactly that transaction from the outside.

What that background means in practice is legible in the CoreWeave contract architecture. The June 2024 announcement — a 200-megawatt, twelve-year colocation agreement with estimated revenues of $3.5 billion — was not primarily an operational achievement. It was a deal. CoreWeave's subsequent option exercises, expanding the relationship to approximately 390 megawatts and $8.7 billion in contracted revenue, were structured with the kind of precision that investment bankers recognize: fixed escalators, defined power densities, construction milestones tied to billing commencement. The $3.3 billion project bond priced in April 2026 — which used those CoreWeave contracts as the underlying credit collateral — was essentially the closing transaction in a series of capital markets moves that began with Sullivan's recruitment. A traditional mining operator might have built those relationships organically over years. Sullivan's team structured them as financings.

The tension, flagged quietly by governance observers, is that running nine data center sites simultaneously, managing construction at Pecos and Muskogee, coordinating grid interconnection across five states, and executing the conversion of bitcoin mining infrastructure to GPU colocation at gigawatt scale is emphatically an operational undertaking. Transaction advisory and infrastructure operations share some vocabulary but relatively little muscle memory.

## The XMS Capital Partnership

James Nygaard joined as Chief Financial Officer in [March 2025](https://investors.corescientific.com/news-releases/news-release-details/core-scientific-appoints-james-nygaard-chief-financial-officer) from the same firm where Sullivan had built his career. At fifty, Nygaard brought approximately thirty years of investment banking experience, including more than a decade at Morgan Stanley, before joining XMS Capital in 2008 as Managing Director and Head of M&A — a position he held until his recruitment to Core Scientific. The two men were colleagues at XMS for roughly six years.

The CEO-CFO dynamic that results from placing two veterans of the same small Chicago boutique in the two most consequential seats of a multi-billion-dollar public company is unusual enough to have attracted governance commentary. The alignment is real: Sullivan and Nygaard share a transaction-centric worldview, speak the same analytical language, and have collaborated long enough to move quickly on capital markets decisions. The April 2026 project bond — priced within weeks of announcement, at terms that validated the CoreWeave contracts as investment-grade-equivalent collateral — is evidence of what that coordination produces. The risk is the mirror image: two executives who spent their careers structuring deals may underweight the grinding operational complexity of managing construction timelines, utility relationships, and site-level workforce issues across a nine-site portfolio. The company's COO, Matt Brown, presumably carries significant weight in bridging that gap.

## The Institutional Memory

Below the C-suite, Core Scientific's operating leadership carries an asymmetric characteristic: several of the most consequential figures have tenures that substantially predate the bankruptcy, giving the company a layer of institutional memory that the executive suite, assembled largely during and after the restructuring, cannot replicate.

Russell Cann, the Chief Development Officer, reached his 9.3-year mark at the snapshot date. He joined when Core Scientific was a startup with Seattle roots and a largely theoretical mining operation, survived the SPAC merger and its attendant strategic confusion, navigated the bankruptcy, and emerged as the company's primary custodian of site-selection, permitting, and grid interconnection knowledge. Those relationships — with utilities, grid operators, county planning boards, and state economic development agencies — are not transferable assets. They exist in Cann's professional network and institutional knowledge. His persistence through both failure and reinvention is either a testament to his adaptability or evidence that Core Scientific's operational infrastructure genuinely depends on continuity that money cannot quickly replace. Probably both.

Todd Duchene, the Executive Vice President and General Counsel, reached 7.1 years at the snapshot, making him the second-longest-tenured executive on the leadership team. Lynn Burgener, the Senior Vice President of Tax and Trade, reached 7.4 years. The presence of a long-tenured tax and trade specialist in senior leadership reflects an underappreciated dimension of Core Scientific's competitive position: the power purchase agreements, site development incentives, and tax treatment of the company's real estate and equipment assets across five states represent years of accumulated structuring work that underpins the financial model.

Larry Kom, the Chief Technology Officer, completes the operating C-suite alongside Brown and Cann. His role — translating the power infrastructure legacy of a mining fleet into the precision requirements of GPU cluster deployments — represents one of the company's most technically demanding transitions. Bitcoin mining hardware tolerates thermal and power management conditions that NVIDIA's H100 and successor GPU clusters emphatically do not.

## Reconstituting the Board

The post-emergence board that took shape in January 2024 was assembled to exit bankruptcy — pragmatic, creditor-aligned, and not particularly calibrated to the governance requirements of a company executing a multi-billion-dollar infrastructure pivot in the public markets. Jordan Levy served as Chairman; Jeff Booth, Yadin Rozov, and Eric Weiss rounded out the initial slate. Elizabeth Crain, co-founder and former Chief Operating Officer of [Moelis & Company](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=CORZ&type=DEF+14A&dateb=&owner=include&count=5), joined in May 2025, bringing institutional investment banking governance experience to a board that had been largely composed of figures from the crypto-adjacent investing world.

The governance stress point came in October 2025, when shareholders voted approximately ten-to-one against the CoreWeave all-stock acquisition. The sequence — board approval in July 2025, organized opposition from Two Seas Capital, decisive shareholder rejection four months later — raised the question of whether the incumbent board had adequately stress-tested the deal's terms, or whether the transaction-centric worldview of the executive suite had permeated the oversight layer as well. The February 2026 cooperation agreement with [Two Seas Capital](https://investors.corescientific.com/news-releases/news-release-details/core-scientific-announces-cooperation-agreement-two-seas-capital) was the explicit acknowledgment: the board required reconstitution to reflect the scale of decisions the company now faced. Three new independent directors would be added in stages — by March 2026, September 2026, and before the 2027 annual meeting — and Jordan Levy announced he would not seek re-election at the 2026 annual meeting. Two Seas agreed to a one-year standstill capping its position at 9.9%.

## The Equinix Credential

The most consequential appointment in the reconstitution came in May 2026, when [Steve Smith joined the board](https://investors.corescientific.com/corporate-governance/board-of-directors). As Chief Executive Officer of Equinix from 2007 to 2018, Smith presided over the company's conversion from a niche colocation operator to the world's largest data center REIT, overseeing its expansion to more than two hundred data centers across five continents and its evolution into the central node of enterprise cloud interconnection. The period Smith ran Equinix — the hyperscale buildout era, the REIT conversion, the disciplined underwriting of long-term colocation contracts — is precisely the institutional period whose lessons are most directly applicable to what Core Scientific is attempting to construct. His current role as CEO of Zayo Group adds contemporary infrastructure operating credibility.

His addition to the board is both an implicit endorsement and an explicit resource. The endorsement is that a former CEO of Equinix — someone who has seen every version of the data center value proposition — looked at Core Scientific's assets, contracts, and development pipeline and concluded the strategy was credible. The resource is that Smith has navigated exactly the governance, capital allocation, and customer-relationship challenges that Core Scientific faces as it scales from a mining operator with some colocation contracts to a genuine data center company with mining operations it is deliberately unwinding.

## The Absent Sponsor

One structural characteristic of Core Scientific's governance deserves emphasis because it is genuinely unusual for a company of this age and complexity: there is no private equity sponsor. Post-bankruptcy equity was distributed to former creditors — noteholders and equipment lenders whose debt converted to equity in the restructuring — creating a dispersed shareholder base with no single controlling party. Two Seas Capital, at approximately 9.9% and capped by standstill, is the closest analog to an activist-owner dynamic, and its influence has been directional rather than operational: the cooperation agreement shaped board composition and removed the failed acquisition overhang, but Two Seas does not appear to be directing day-to-day capital allocation decisions.

The absence of a sponsor creates both freedom and exposure. The freedom is that Sullivan has latitude to execute the HPC pivot without a financial sponsor extracting fees, competing for board seats, or managing toward a fixed-horizon exit. The exposure is that the accountability structure — dispersed institutional and retail shareholders, a reconstituting board, an activist minority — provides less concentrated oversight than a PE-backed governance model would. Whether that produces better or worse outcomes at Core Scientific will depend substantially on whether the board reconstitution delivers the independent judgment it was designed to provide, and whether the company's operational execution justifies the transactional credibility that built its current architecture.

chapters.title: The CoreWeave Dependency and the Path to Customer Diversification
chapters.body:
## One Customer, One Bet

No commercial relationship in American digital infrastructure is quite as concentrated — or as consequential — as the one between Core Scientific and CoreWeave. As of the snapshot date, CoreWeave accounts for effectively all of Core Scientific's contracted high-performance computing revenue, a dependency that is simultaneously the company's greatest financial asset and its most significant structural vulnerability.

The relationship was constructed in four discrete tranches across less than a year. On June 3, 2024, five months after Core Scientific emerged from Chapter 11, the two companies announced a landmark 200-megawatt, twelve-year HPC colocation agreement with estimated cumulative revenue of $3.5 billion — roughly $17.50 per watt over the contract term, reflecting the scarcity premium of immediately available, grid-connected, high-density data center space in a market starved for AI compute infrastructure. The initial contract alone was larger than any deal Core Scientific had signed in its history. CoreWeave then exercised the first of two embedded expansion options on June 25, 2024, adding approximately 70 megawatts and $1.225 billion in projected revenue. A second and final option, exercised October 22, 2024, contributed a further 120 megawatts and $2.0 billion. A February 2025 expansion at the Denton, Texas Polaris campus added $1.2 billion incrementally, bringing the total relationship to approximately 390 megawatts under contract and approximately $8.7 billion in cumulative committed revenue across twelve-year terms.

By any measure, the commercial architecture of that relationship represents an extraordinary vote of confidence from CoreWeave in Core Scientific's operational capabilities. It also represents, by design, an almost total reorientation of the business around a single customer.

## CoreWeave: The Anchor and Its Weight

Understanding the concentration risk requires understanding CoreWeave itself. The company was founded as Atlantic Crypto in 2017 and pivoted to GPU cloud computing as NVIDIA's H100 chips became the scarce resource of the AI era. NVIDIA became a major equity investor, and CoreWeave built its reputation supplying GPU compute to some of the largest AI laboratories in the world — its customers include OpenAI. CoreWeave went public on Nasdaq under the ticker CRWV in March 2025, one of the most anticipated technology listings of the year, and has grown into one of the fastest-scaling cloud infrastructure providers in the sector. Its capital intensity is extreme: building and operating GPU clusters at scale requires continuous access to debt and equity markets, and CoreWeave's own financial health directly determines its capacity to fund the Core Scientific expansion program on schedule.

The commercial contracts between the two companies are structured as Core Scientific providing powered, cooled shell space — the infrastructure landlord model — while CoreWeave installs and operates the NVIDIA GPU hardware. The economics are deliberately simple: Core Scientific receives fixed payments tied to delivered megawatts, insulated from CoreWeave's utilization rates or its own customers' demand patterns. The twelve-year terms lock in revenue regardless of what happens to AI pricing or hyperscaler competition.
