As Adam Sullivan has noted on earnings calls, the colocation model puts Core Scientific in a fundamentally different risk position than a hyperscaler or GPU cloud operator: it is closer to a toll-road operator than a technology company.

That insulation has limits. CoreWeave's financial health matters to Core Scientific in ways that go beyond standard counterparty credit risk. The April 2026 $3.3 billion project bond — priced at 7.75%, due 2031, generating approximately $2.9 billion in net proceeds — was explicitly collateralized by the CoreWeave contract cash flows across six Core Scientific sites. The bond's terms and execution demonstrate that the capital markets view CoreWeave's twelve-year commitments as sufficiently bankable to support one of the largest single infrastructure debt raises in the AI sector to date. That validation is significant: it means Core Scientific's ability to fund its own expansion program is, in a structural sense, contingent on CoreWeave maintaining the creditworthiness that makes those contracts attractive as project finance collateral.

The failed acquisition attempt of July through October 2025 sharpened the codependency into sharper relief. When CoreWeave announced a definitive all-stock acquisition of Core Scientific on July 7, 2025, shareholders read the offer as undervalued — an attempt by a customer to internalize landlord economics at below-market terms. The rejection was emphatic: at the October 30, 2025 stockholder vote, approximately 203.5 million shares voted against, 20.8 million in favor, and 21.6 million abstained, a roughly ten-to-one defeat. The commercial contracts remained intact through the termination. What the episode revealed, however, was that CoreWeave's preferred resolution to the concentration risk was consolidation rather than diversification — an option Core Scientific's owners refused, but which illustrates the degree to which both parties understood they had created an unusually interdependent commercial structure.

## The Revenue Trough and the Ramp

The financial mechanics of the transition put the concentration risk in quantitative context. In FY2025, Core Scientific reported total revenue of $319.0 million — a 37.5 percent decline from FY2024's $510.7 million, a trough year reflecting the deliberate destruction of the legacy mining base in favor of a higher-margin successor model. Self-mining contributed $229.2 million; HPC colocation contributed $65.4 million; hosted mining added $24.4 million.

By Q1 2026, the ramp had become unmistakable. With 243 megawatts billing, colocation revenue reached $77.5 million in a single quarter — an annualized run rate of approximately $310 million, already 4.7 times the entirety of FY2025 colocation revenue. Gross margins on the CoreWeave contracts have been guided to the 80–85 percent range, raised from the original 75–80 percent guide as operational efficiencies became apparent. Q1 2026 marked Core Scientific's first quarter of positive Adjusted EBITDA in the HPC transition era, at $4.4 million on $115.2 million in total revenue.

| Period | Colocation Revenue | MW Billing | Blended Gross Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2024 | (transitional) | <50 MW (est.) | — |
| FY2025 | $65.4M | Ramping | ~12% (blended) |
| Q1 2026 | $77.5M | 243 MW | Guided 80–85% at scale |
| Target (late summer 2026) | — | 450+ MW | — |
| Target (early 2027) | — | 590 MW | — |

The hosted mining business — the third segment — tells a simpler story of managed decline. Core Scientific's hosted mining model provided physical infrastructure to third-party bitcoin miners who operated their own application-specific integrated circuit hardware on Core Scientific's power and cooling systems. The $24.4 million in FY2025 revenue from that model represents a fraction of what the same megawatts will generate once converted to HPC colocation, and management has been explicit about the intent to wind down the segment entirely as conversion proceeds.

## The Diversification Imperative

Beyond the financial mechanics, the concentration question is ultimately a strategic one: how long can a company whose entire contracted HPC revenue flows from a single customer sustain the valuation premium of a mature infrastructure operator?

Industry analysts have cited Microsoft and Google as the most likely candidates for a second or third anchor HPC tenant, with Core Scientific's greenfield development pipelines at Pecos, Texas — a 1.5-gigawatt long-term target — and Port Muskogee, Oklahoma — a 100-megawatt Phase 1 under construction with a 1.5-gigawatt pipeline — as the logical vessels for any such relationship. The Pecos site in particular, with its proximity to low-cost West Texas power and its scale ambitions, is the kind of asset a hyperscaler looking to secure AI infrastructure capacity would find attractive. As of the May 23, 2026 snapshot, however, no contracts with Microsoft, Google, or any other HPC customer beyond CoreWeave had been publicly disclosed.

The Hunt County, Texas development — announced in 2026 and targeted at approximately 430 megawatts of gross capacity — adds another pipeline asset to the portfolio, with its roughly $700 million acquisition forming part of the $2 billion guided capital expenditure for 2026. The identity of any planned HPC tenant for Hunt County had not been publicly disclosed as of the snapshot date.

The arithmetic of diversification is straightforward. A second anchor tenant at, say, 200 megawatts under a twelve-year contract at comparable economics would add approximately $3.5 billion in contracted revenue and reduce CoreWeave's share of the contracted backlog from effectively 100 percent to roughly 70 percent — meaningfully improving the company's negotiating posture on future contract renewals, the project bond covenant structure, and the risk-adjusted valuation that institutional investors are willing to assign to the revenue stream. Two anchor tenants would push the story closer to the multi-tenant colocation model that commands Equinix-like multiples in public markets.

Until that second contract materializes, Core Scientific's customer diversification strategy consists primarily of optionality — greenfield capacity that could house future tenants, analyst speculation about Microsoft and Google, and the demonstrated ability to execute at scale that Sullivan has argued makes the company the natural partner for any hyperscaler looking for a proven infrastructure landlord. Whether that optionality converts to executed contracts, and on what timeline, is the central open question in the investment case as the company exits its transition trough and approaches the profitability that its contracted backlog has long promised.

chapters.title: The AI Infrastructure Land Grab: Core Scientific vs. Mining Peers, Data Center Incumbents, and Private Challengers
chapters.body:
## Three Arenas, One Race

The most instructive way to understand Core Scientific's competitive position is to separate the company it used to be — one of North America's largest bitcoin miners — from the company it is actively becoming: a high-power-density AI colocation landlord. Those two identities put CORZ in competition with radically different peer groups simultaneously. Against its former bitcoin mining peers, Core Scientific is the defector, the company that chose landlord economics over mining economics when the data made that choice obvious. Against the established data center operators it hopes to emulate — Equinix, Digital Realty — it is the challenger, arriving with owned assets and operational credibility but without decades of customer relationships and investment-grade credit history. Against the private infrastructure developers and hyperscaler self-builders crowding the same AI power markets, it is racing to lock in interconnection assets and long-term contracts before the window narrows.

## Mining Peers: The Defectors and the Holdouts

Among publicly traded bitcoin miners navigating the AI pivot, Core Scientific occupies a position that Bernstein analysts have characterised as the sector "blueprint" — the company that moved fastest, signed the largest contract, and demonstrated that mining infrastructure could command data centre economics. The comparison to Riot Platforms (RIOT) is unavoidable.

Riot operates the single largest bitcoin mining site in the United States at Rockdale, Texas, where its Whinstone campus runs more than 700 megawatts of gross capacity. That scale is formidable; Rockdale dwarfs any individual Core Scientific site. But scale alone does not determine the value of the pivot. Riot's business model at Rockdale has historically leaned on power curtailment revenue — selling contracted power capacity back to the Texas grid during periods of peak demand — rather than maximising uptime for sustained computing workloads. That model is structurally different from Core Scientific's colocation landlord approach, in which tenants such as CoreWeave pay a fixed price per kilowatt for guaranteed, uninterrupted power delivery to run dense GPU clusters. Curtailment and colocation are partially incompatible: a landlord cannot intermittently sell its tenant's power back to the grid. As of the May 2026 snapshot, Riot had announced AI/HPC pivot intentions but remained at a materially earlier stage of contract execution than Core Scientific. Bernstein's "blueprint" characterisation captures the sequencing precisely: Riot must now follow a path that Core Scientific has already validated — identifying which sites to convert, which power is unencumbered by curtailment obligations, and which customers will underwrite multi-year colocation agreements at data centre pricing.

Marathon Digital (MARA) presents an even starker contrast. Marathon is primarily a bitcoin treasury company — the largest institutional holder of bitcoin among publicly listed miners — with a mining fleet that serves, in part, to accumulate additional coin. Its AI pivot ambitions, through the snapshot date, remained nascent. Marathon's market capitalisation of roughly $5–6 billion places it in a comparable range to Core Scientific's approximately $8 billion, yet the strategic positioning diverges sharply: where [CORZ](https://investors.corescientific.com/) is systematically converting its revenue base toward long-term contracted colocation income, MARA's earnings remain tightly coupled to bitcoin price and network hash-rate dynamics. The overlap between Marathon's and Core Scientific's institutional shareholder bases — funds holding both for exposure to bitcoin-adjacent infrastructure — creates a latent re-allocation dynamic. As CORZ's colocation revenue scales, those investors must decide whether Marathon offers a credible AI growth story or simply leveraged bitcoin exposure in infrastructure packaging.

IREN (Iris Energy) is the mining-peer comparison that analysts find most analytically useful after Core Scientific itself. IREN has pursued a GPU colocation strategy centred on owned data centres, and Bernstein rates both companies "Outperform," implying conviction that the AI infrastructure transition is real for each. The similarities are genuine: IREN operates owned facilities, targets GPU-cloud operators as anchor tenants, and has executed initial customer agreements. The differences are of stage and scale. Core Scientific's contracted colocation backlog — approximately $8.7 billion over twelve years from CoreWeave alone — is orders of magnitude larger than IREN's equivalent position at the snapshot date. Core Scientific commands 724 megawatts of operational capacity across nine sites; IREN's comparable footprint is smaller and its customer relationships remain at an earlier stage of execution. The gap in capital structure sophistication is equally material: the April 2026 [$3.3 billion project bond](https://investors.corescientific.com/news-releases/news-release-details/core-scientific-prices-33-billion-senior-secured-project-bonds), collateralised against the CoreWeave contract cash flows, is a financing mechanism that presupposes a multi-year contracted revenue base that IREN has not yet assembled. CleanSpark, by contrast, has remained closer to a pure-play bitcoin mining posture, making it a useful control in the peer group — the company that did not pivot — rather than a direct competitive threat in the AI colocation market.

## Data Centre Incumbents: The Owned-Asset Moat

Against the established data centre operators and REITs — Equinix, Digital Realty, Iron Mountain Digital — Core Scientific starts from a position of structural advantage on two dimensions that the incumbents cannot easily replicate: owned real estate and existing grid interconnections.

Equinix and Digital Realty operate largely on leased land or owned campuses optimised for carrier-neutral interconnection density — the ability to cross-connect carriers, cloud on-ramps, and enterprise networks in dense metropolitan facilities. For AI training and inference workloads that require hundreds of megawatts of dense GPU capacity at a single site, the carrier-neutral interconnection premium that underpins Equinix's roughly 20x EV/EBITDA valuation is largely irrelevant. What matters is uninterrupted bulk power, advanced thermal management, and physical proximity to high-voltage transmission infrastructure in power-rich markets.

Core Scientific's sites in Auburn, Alabama; Dalton, Georgia; Denton, Texas; and the development pipelines at Pecos and Muskogee were engineered to deliver power at the densities that bitcoin mining demands — conditions that now align with the 50–100 kilowatts per rack that modern GPU clusters require. Obtaining a new grid interconnection for a greenfield data centre in a power-constrained U.S. market currently requires three to five years in most jurisdictions. Core Scientific's portfolio of existing interconnections represents, in effect, a non-replicable call option on scarce transmission capacity assembled during a period when power capacity was cheap and bitcoin mining was the only buyer willing to absorb it.

The cost-basis argument reinforces the moat. Converting an existing bitcoin mining facility to GPU-ready AI colocation costs materially less per megawatt than building a comparable greenfield data centre: the land is owned, the grid connection exists, and the thermal and electrical infrastructure is partially in place. That conversion cost advantage translates directly into competitive lease rates — Core Scientific can offer GPU-cloud tenants lower all-in costs per kilowatt than a greenfield developer while still generating the 80–85% gross margins that management has guided for the CoreWeave contracts. Private challengers such as Crusoe Energy, Vantage Data Centres, and DataBank are formidable operators, but they are building at market-rate land and interconnection costs, compressing their margin room relative to a landlord that acquired its power position when bitcoin miners were the marginal buyer.

## The Hyperscaler Question

The structural threat facing any third-party colocation operator is hyperscaler self-build. Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon collectively announced hundreds of billions of dollars in data centre capital expenditure commitments in 2025 and 2026. If those companies internalise AI compute capacity at scale, the addressable market for companies such as Core Scientific narrows.

The counterargument rests on workload economics and capital prioritisation. Hyperscalers prefer to own infrastructure for their core, long-lived workloads — general-purpose compute, object storage, internal services — where owned infrastructure compounds economic advantage over time. For burst AI capacity, rapidly evolving GPU generations, and GPU-cloud operators such as CoreWeave that serve frontier model developers including OpenAI, the calculus differs. CoreWeave's preference for third-party colocation reflects a deliberate capital allocation choice: outsource real estate and power delivery, concentrate capital on GPU procurement and high-performance networking. The anchor relationship with Core Scientific is the output of that decision.

The limit of that preference is the key uncertainty. If AI infrastructure demand growth remains as steep as the 2025–2026 commitment cycle implies, the demand-supply imbalance for high-power-density data centre capacity could persist for years. If hyperscalers accelerate self-build faster than expected and GPU-cloud operators face pricing pressure from the resulting supply addition, the structural case for third-party colocation erodes at the margin. For now, the evidence of the $8.7 billion CoreWeave contract and the market validation demonstrated by the $3.3 billion project bond — among the largest single AI infrastructure debt raises of 2026 — suggests that institutional capital markets believe the demand-supply gap is real, durable, and material enough to underwrite infrastructure finance at scale. The investment banks that structured and distributed that bond, and the credit investors who bought it, were making an explicit bet on the same competitive moat that Adam Sullivan articulated when he accepted the presidency of a bankrupt bitcoin miner in the spring of 2023.

chapters.title: Event Log and Forward Catalysts: The Timeline That Defined Core Scientific's Second Act
chapters.body:
## The First Twenty-Eight Months: A Chronology of Reinvention

Core Scientific's second act has compressed what ordinarily takes a decade of infrastructure repositioning into less than three years. From the January 24, 2024 Nasdaq relisting to the $3.3 billion project bond that closed the spring of 2026, the company executed a succession of discrete, high-stakes transactions that, taken together, transformed a bankrupt bitcoin miner into a credible AI infrastructure landlord. Each event in that sequence was both a consequence of the one before and a precondition for the one that followed.

| Date | Event | Strategic Significance |
|------|-------|----------------------|
| Jan 24, 2024 | Chapter 11 emergence; Nasdaq relisting as CORZ | Clean balance sheet, ~$400M debt eliminated; HPC pivot strategy in place from Day 1 |
| Jun 3, 2024 | CoreWeave 200 MW anchor contract, $3.5B cumulative revenue | Proof of concept for the colocation model; gave the company a creditworthy anchor tenant |
| Jun 25, 2024 | First CoreWeave option: ~70 MW, ~$1.225B | Rapid validation that CoreWeave wanted more capacity; accelerated conversion capital allocation |
| Aug 2024 | $400M convertible notes at 3.00%, due Sep 2029 | Bridge capital for HPC conversion capex ahead of larger project bond |
| Oct 22, 2024 | Second CoreWeave option: ~120 MW, ~$2.0B | Total relationship reaches ~390 MW, ~$8.7B contracted; scale justified greenfield development |
| Nov 2024 | Port Muskogee groundbreaking (100 MW Phase 1; 1.5 GW pipeline) | First purpose-built AI data center campus outside existing sites |
| Feb 2025 | Denton (Polaris) expansion, $1.2B additional CoreWeave capacity | CoreWeave deepens commitment at flagship Texas site |
| Mar 2025 | James Nygaard appointed CFO | XMS Capital duo solidified; transaction-centric finance leadership in place |
| May 2025 | Crain added to board | Incremental governance reinforcement ahead of a contested summer |
| Jul 7, 2025 | CoreWeave all-stock acquisition agreement announced | The event that forced shareholders to define what independence was worth |
| Oct 30, 2025 | Merger terminated; shareholder vote 203.5M against, 20.8M for | Most consequential vote in company's post-emergence history; independence preserved |
| Feb 18, 2026 | Two Seas Capital cooperation agreement | Board reconstitution mandated; activist standstill capped at 9.9% |
| Apr 2026 | $3.3B project bonds at 7.75%, due 2031 | Largest AI infrastructure debt raise of the year; contracts proven bankable as project collateral |
| May 2026 | Steve Smith (former Equinix CEO) joins board | Single most operationally credentialed director addition in company's history |

## The Acquisition That Wasn't: Ten-to-One Against

No event in Core Scientific's post-emergence history was more consequential — or more illuminating about the company's perceived value — than the three months between CoreWeave's July 7, 2025 acquisition announcement and the October 30, 2025 vote that killed it.

CoreWeave's offer was all-stock. The strategic logic was straightforward: CoreWeave wanted to control the real estate underlying its largest data center footprint and eliminate the landlord-tenant intermediary. For Core Scientific shareholders, the offer posed an existential question — whether the company's value was more fully realized as an asset inside CoreWeave's capital structure or as an independent operator scaling a contracted revenue base toward a data center multiple.

Shareholders answered with near-unanimity. The final count — approximately 203.5 million shares voted against, 20.8 million in favor, 21.6 million abstained — was a roughly ten-to-one rejection. Two Seas Capital, which had accumulated a position approaching the 9.9% threshold, organized the opposition and argued that the all-stock consideration drastically undervalued Core Scientific's $8.7 billion contracted revenue backlog and the optionality embedded in the Pecos and Muskogee development pipelines.

The vote's significance extends beyond the deal itself. It established that Core Scientific's shareholder base believes the company is worth more as an independent colocation operator than as a captive subsidiary — and that the twelve-year contractual relationship with CoreWeave provides sufficient revenue certainty to justify the execution risk of independence. It also crystallized a governance irony: the board that approved the deal in July was overruled by the shareholders it nominally represented, triggering the Two Seas cooperation agreement and the boardroom reconstitution that followed. The commercial contracts with CoreWeave were unaffected by the termination, preserving the $8.7 billion revenue base regardless of the governance outcome.

## Bitcoin as Backward-Looking Catalyst

The strategic urgency of Core Scientific's HPC pivot is inseparable from bitcoin's price trajectory through the transition period. Bitcoin's recovery from its 2022–2023 lows — the very collapse that pushed Core Scientific into bankruptcy — created a transitional period in which self-mining remained economically meaningful even as management was structurally dismantling it. Self-mining contributed $229.2 million of FY2025 revenue, the largest single segment, providing cash flow that partially subsidized the conversion capital expenditure.

The internal rate of return calculation for converting megawatts from mining to colocation is not complicated, but bitcoin price sensitivity makes the timing decision consequential. A 200-megawatt bitcoin mining deployment, at prevailing 2024–2025 economics, generated perhaps $50–80 million in annual gross profit at current hash prices — a figure that fluctuates with every difficulty adjustment and every swing in bitcoin's dollar price. The same 200 megawatts contracted to CoreWeave at the guided 80–85% gross margin on a twelve-year fixed-price agreement generates $120–160 million in annual gross profit at maturity, with near-zero operating leverage variation. The spread between those two outcomes — roughly 2–3 times the annual return, with dramatically lower volatility — is the quantitative engine of Sullivan's strategy.

As bitcoin prices remained elevated through 2024–2025, the opportunity cost of converting megawatts from mining to colocation was real but, in Sullivan's framing, clearly dominated by the long-term colocation return. The self-mining wind-down to one or two sites by end-2026 reflects management's view that at scale, the IRR of colocation exceeds mining across virtually any plausible bitcoin price scenario.

## Forward Catalysts: The Milestones That Will Define 2026–2027

As of the May 23, 2026 snapshot, the forward catalyst stack is unusually dense and time-specific.

The most immediate is the megawatt billing ramp. With 243 megawatts billing in Q1 2026 at a quarterly colocation revenue rate of $77.5 million, the path to 450-plus megawatts by late summer 2026 and 590 megawatts by early 2027 would drive annualized colocation revenue approaching $400–500 million — a figure that, at 80–85% gross margins, produces Adjusted EBITDA approaching $320–425 million from the colocation segment alone. The Q1 2026 positive Adjusted EBITDA of $4.4 million — the first in the transition era — marked the inflection; the trajectory through the remainder of 2026 will determine whether consensus FY2027 EBITDA estimates of $600–800 million are conservative or aspirational.

Three site-specific milestones carry particular weight. Muskogee Phase 1, the 100-megawatt first segment of a 1.5-gigawatt development at Port Muskogee, Oklahoma, is the company's first purpose-built AI data center outside its legacy bitcoin mining footprint; its commissioning timeline will test Core Scientific's greenfield construction capabilities at a moment when every day of delay represents foregone contracted revenue. Hunt County, Texas — a roughly 430-megawatt gross development announced in 2026 whose tenant identity had not been publicly disclosed as of the snapshot date — is the clearest signal that Core Scientific is diversifying beyond CoreWeave; the identity of that customer, when disclosed, will be among the most consequential news events of the year. The self-mining wind-down, if completed on the guided 2026 timeline, removes the last structural drag on blended gross margins and simplifies the equity story to a single, high-margin colocation thesis.

The addition of Steve Smith to the board in May 2026 is itself a soft catalyst of a different kind. As the architect of Equinix's REIT conversion and the executive who scaled that company from a domestic exchange operator to a 200-site global interconnection platform, Smith brings a specific institutional template: the playbook for converting a niche infrastructure operator into a diversified, investment-grade data center landlord commanding a premium multiple. Whether Core Scientific follows that template — or whether the CoreWeave dependency and the complexity of its capital structure permanently distinguish it from its REIT-class peers — is the defining strategic question that the next eighteen months of execution will begin to answer.

chapters.title: Operational Know-How as Competitive Moat: Power Engineering, Site Operations, and Infrastructure IP
chapters.body:
## The Moat That Cannot Be Photocopied

Core Scientific's competitive advantages resist the standard taxonomy applied to technology companies. There are no dominant patents, no proprietary algorithms whose value compounds with each additional user, no network effects in the conventional sense. What the company possessed instead, as of the 2026-05-23 snapshot, was something harder to replicate and in some respects more durable: nine sites, 724 megawatts of grid-connected capacity across five states, and an operations organization that had spent years learning, at genuine commercial scale, how to keep extreme-density power environments running continuously. That combination of physical infrastructure and embedded institutional knowledge constituted a moat whose depth was measured not in patent claims but in interconnection queues and thermal management scar tissue.

## The Engineering Reality of Facility Conversion

The conversion of a bitcoin mining facility into a GPU colocation site is not a matter of clearing out ASIC racks and replacing them with GPU servers. The engineering gap between the two use cases is substantial, and Core Scientific's accumulated experience navigating it represents one of its most defensible advantages.

A purpose-built bitcoin mining building is typically a single-story, wide-span structure optimized for forced-air cooling of ASIC hardware running at six to ten kilowatts per rack. The architectural logic is simple: maximize air throughput, minimize humidity exposure, and pack as many hashing units as possible into a given footprint. Power distribution infrastructure in these facilities was designed for uniform, predictable loads — mining hardware draws what it draws, continuously, without the surge dynamics associated with GPU training workloads.

GPU colocation for AI training flips those parameters. NVIDIA H100 and H200 clusters run at thirty to fifty or more kilowatts per rack, require liquid cooling loops rather than simple forced-air configurations, impose higher demands on the uninterruptible power supply architecture, and generate localized heat densities that can overwhelm ceiling heights and floor loading tolerances designed for a lighter era. The mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) scope of a mining-to-GPU conversion touches nearly every building system: medium-voltage switchgear upgrades, chilled water or direct-to-chip liquid cooling distribution, supplemental structural reinforcement, generator tie-in reconfiguration, and the integration of facility management systems capable of monitoring per-rack power consumption and thermal performance simultaneously across hundreds of cabinets.

Core Scientific executed this conversion across multiple sites and hundreds of megawatts — with 243 megawatts actively billing CoreWeave by the first quarter of 2026 and a target of 590 megawatts converted by early 2027. Each completed conversion yielded an engineering library of specifications, contractor relationships, equipment lead times, and failure modes that the organization carries forward. A competitor without that history would be buying speed from consultants rather than drawing on internalized expertise; the difference in construction velocity and contingency management is not trivial at billion-dollar project scales.

## The Interconnection Portfolio as Irreplaceable Asset

Perhaps more durable than any specific engineering knowledge is the grid interconnection portfolio itself. Core Scientific managed 724 megawatts of contracted grid capacity across sites in Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, North Carolina, North Dakota, and Texas as of the snapshot date. Each of those interconnections represents a completed negotiation with a regional transmission organization — including the Southwest Power Pool, the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, PJM, or the relevant utility — that took years to advance through study queues, cost allocation processes, and regulatory approval cycles.

The lead times for new large-scale grid interconnections have lengthened dramatically as AI data center demand has accelerated. Independent analyses of FERC interconnection queues have documented average timelines of four to seven years for projects seeking transmission-level interconnections above 100 megawatts, with some markets reporting backlogs that extend the effective waiting period further still. Core Scientific's existing interconnections represent those years of queue time already spent — a sunk cost that cannot be compressed by capital alone. A new entrant seeking to replicate a comparable footprint of grid-connected, power-dense sites in competitive markets would face both the monetary cost of interconnection and the irreducible time cost of the queue, a combination that insulates Core Scientific's position for the duration of the current AI infrastructure build cycle.

The company's relationships with multiple RTOs and utilities across five states also carry embedded regulatory knowledge: understanding of each jurisdiction's tariff structures, demand response program requirements, curtailment protocols, and the informal norms that govern how large industrial customers negotiate capacity expansions. That accumulated relationship capital does not appear on the balance sheet.

## Operational Systems and Uptime Obligations

CoreWeave's colocation agreements with Core Scientific carry service level requirements reflective of the end-use case: CoreWeave itself serves AI training workloads for operators including OpenAI, where compute interruptions translate directly into customer cost and reputational exposure. Meeting those SLAs requires facility management capabilities substantially beyond what bitcoin mining operations demanded.

Core Scientific operates centralized monitoring infrastructure capable of tracking power utilization, thermal performance, cooling system status, and generator readiness across its distributed site portfolio. The company has not disclosed the precise architecture of its facility management systems in detail sufficient to determine what proportion is proprietary software development versus integrated commercial platforms — building automation systems from vendors such as Schneider Electric, Siemens, or Johnson Controls are standard industry components. What can be assessed is that the operational discipline required to maintain uptime SLAs across a 243-megawatt live customer deployment, while simultaneously managing conversion construction at adjacent or co-located infrastructure, demands organizational process maturity that is not quickly improvised.

## Patents, Trade Secrets, and the IP Framework

Core Scientific has not built its competitive position on a formal patent portfolio. Bitcoin mining companies as a category held few technology patents — the competitive dynamics of the sector rewarded scale and cost efficiency over innovation protection, and the relevant hardware intellectual property resided with ASIC manufacturers such as Bitmain and MicroBT rather than with operators. As of the snapshot date, no significant patent filings related to cooling architecture, power management systems, or data center conversion processes had been publicly associated with Core Scientific.

The operative IP framework was instead one of trade secrets and process knowledge: the accumulated specifications, engineering drawings, contractor evaluation frameworks, utility negotiation strategies, and operational runbooks that constitute the company's conversion methodology. These assets are difficult to protect through formal registration and equally difficult to replicate through hiring alone, because the knowledge is organizational rather than individual — embedded in teams and processes rather than in any single engineer's expertise. That structural characteristic, more than any filing with the USPTO, defined the durability of Core Scientific's operational moat as it scaled toward a gigawatt-class AI infrastructure platform.

chapters.title: Six Structural Risks: Customer Concentration, Execution Scale, Capital Structure, Bitcoin Residual, Governance, and Regulatory
chapters.body:
## Risk 1: Customer Concentration — The CoreWeave Monogamy Problem

Core Scientific's strategic reinvention rests on a single commercial relationship. CoreWeave accounts for effectively all of the company's contracted high-performance computing revenue — approximately $8.7 billion over twelve years across roughly 390 megawatts of capacity — and the $3.3 billion project bond priced in April 2026 was itself structured around CoreWeave contract cash flows as the primary collateral. That bond transaction, widely described as one of the largest single infrastructure debt raises in the AI sector, was simultaneously a validation of CoreWeave's creditworthiness and a structural amplifier of the concentration risk. The two companies are now financially intertwined to a degree that makes simple counterparty risk analysis inadequate.

The scenarios that matter are not binary default events but degraded states. CoreWeave's own customer base is heavily weighted toward OpenAI, and any material deterioration in that relationship — through OpenAI building owned compute, signing preferential capacity agreements with Microsoft Azure, or shifting inference workloads to alternative infrastructure — would reduce the GPU utilization rates that justify CoreWeave's capacity expansion. A CoreWeave that is growing more slowly is not a CoreWeave that defaults on its Core Scientific lease obligations; the contracts are structured as fixed-capacity payments rather than utilization-linked revenue. But a CoreWeave under financial pressure would inevitably seek to renegotiate the economics of agreements whose cost structure was set during a period of maximum AI infrastructure scarcity.

The failed acquisition attempt of July–October 2025 revealed a darker scenario: that CoreWeave itself could seek to internalize the landlord economics by buying Core Scientific outright. The all-stock deal, rejected by shareholders by approximately ten to one, was structured in a way that would have transferred the contracted revenue streams from Core Scientific's balance sheet to CoreWeave's. The commercial contracts survived the termination intact, but the episode demonstrated that CoreWeave does not regard the colocation relationship as purely arm's-length. A future acquisition attempt — by CoreWeave, or by a hyperscaler acquiring CoreWeave — could renew pressure on those contract terms in ways a standalone Core Scientific is better positioned to resist.

The $3.3 billion project bond matures in 2031. Annual debt service on that instrument at 7.75% runs to approximately $256 million per year in interest alone. CoreWeave's contracted revenue at full buildout is designed to cover those obligations with headroom, but any gap — from delayed megawatt delivery, contract dispute, or CoreWeave credit deterioration — would cascade directly to the project bond's coverage ratios and, ultimately, to Core Scientific's refinancing capacity.

## Risk 2: Execution at Scale — $2 Billion in One Year Across Six Sites

Core Scientific is attempting something with few precedents in the digital infrastructure sector: the simultaneous conversion and greenfield development of six large-scale data center sites within a twelve-month capital deployment window. Guided capital expenditure for 2026 alone is approximately $2 billion, including roughly $700 million associated with the Hunt County, Texas site acquisition and the Polaris/Muskogee purchase. The company has not built a data center from greenfield in its operating history; it has converted existing mining infrastructure. Muskogee's Port site, with a 1.5-gigawatt long-term pipeline, is a different category of construction undertaking.

The equipment procurement bottlenecks that define this risk are structural rather than idiosyncratic. High-power electrical switchgear — the transformers, switchboards, and busway systems that distribute power at densities of 20 to 30 kilowatts per rack — carry lead times measured in eighteen to thirty-six months from major manufacturers including ABB, Eaton, and Schneider Electric, all of whom are managing order books distorted by a global wave of data center construction. Liquid cooling infrastructure, required for the dense NVIDIA GPU configurations CoreWeave deploys, faces similar supply constraints. A six-site simultaneous program amplifies these procurement risks: the company is competing with hyperscalers for the same constrained components, without the purchasing leverage of an Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure.

Grid interconnection timelines represent the most binary execution risk. Core Scientific's operational advantage — existing transmission interconnections in power-rich markets — is most pronounced at its legacy sites. Greenfield development at Pecos and Muskogee requires new interconnection agreements with ERCOT and SPP respectively, navigating FERC-reformed interconnection queues that have seen processing times increase materially since the 2023 Order 2023 reforms. A twelve-month delay in a single large interconnection agreement could push a 300-megawatt billing milestone to the right by a full year, reducing 2027 revenue recognition by approximately $180 to $240 million at the guided margin structure.

Core Scientific's Q1 2026 milestone — 243 megawatts billing, up from 160 megawatts at year-end 2025 — demonstrates that the conversion engine is functioning. But the distance between 243 megawatts and the 590-megawatt target for early 2027 is larger than what has been accomplished to date, and it involves more complex construction programs at newer sites.

## Risk 3: Capital Structure Complexity — Three Layers, One Revenue Stream

The capital structure Core Scientific has assembled is functional but fragile at the margins. Senior secured project bonds of $3.3 billion at 7.75%, due 2031, sit at the top of the waterfall, backed by CoreWeave contract cash flows and site-level assets. Below them, $1.06 billion in 3.00% convertible notes due September 2029 represent an unsecured obligation that will require either refinancing in the debt markets or conversion to equity — at approximately 90.93 shares per $1,000 principal — before their maturity date. At the snapshot date, the total share count implied by full conversion of the convertible notes approaches 96 million shares, a dilution of approximately 10 to 12 percent against the current outstanding float depending on the reference date. The warrant liabilities — issued in the January 2024 bankruptcy reorganization and carried at $936.1 million fair value at December 31, 2025 — add a third layer of non-cash volatility that routinely overwhelms reported net income in either direction.

The most acute maturity risk is the September 2029 convertible notes. The refinancing window for those instruments opens in 2027–2028, in a credit environment that cannot be predicted from a 2026 vantage point. If Core Scientific's HPC buildout is executing as planned, the company will enter that refinancing window with demonstrated EBITDA of $600 million or more (per consensus estimates), strong coverage ratios on the project bonds, and access to investment-grade-adjacent credit markets. If execution has slipped, the refinancing could require equity issuance at dilutive prices or a return to high-yield markets at material cost.

## Risk 4: Bitcoin Residual — A $229 Million Revenue Stream Exposed to Halving Math

Self-mining contributed $229.2 million in FY2025 revenue, representing the largest single segment even as management characterized the year as a transition trough. Core Scientific has committed to consolidating self-mining to one or two sites by end-2026, but the conversion timeline is contingent on HPC buildout velocity. Until the displacement is complete, the company carries meaningful bitcoin price exposure.

A 50 percent decline in bitcoin prices from levels prevailing at the snapshot date would reduce self-mining revenue by roughly $100 to $115 million on an annualized basis, net of the modest variable cost savings from reduced power consumption. That revenue shortfall would not threaten debt service — the project bonds are backed by CoreWeave contract cash flows, not mining revenues — but it would reduce the operating cash buffer available to fund construction cost overruns or bridge delays in CoreWeave reimbursement timing. The FY2025 pattern, in which $279.2 million in capital expenditure was partially offset by $226.2 million in CoreWeave partnership reimbursements, illustrates the dependence on reimbursement timing matching deployment cadence. Bitcoin revenue serves as the margin of safety in that timing arithmetic.

## Risk 5: Governance in Transition — Bankers Managing a Construction Company

The Two Seas cooperation agreement of February 2026 was an implicit acknowledgment that the post-bankruptcy board had not kept pace with the governance demands of a company deploying $2 billion in capital annually. Three new director seats are being added in stages — by March 2026, September 2026, and before the 2027 annual meeting — against a backdrop of Chairman Jordan Levy's announced departure and a board that had approved the CoreWeave all-stock acquisition by a margin shareholders rejected ten to one.

The more structural concern is management depth. Sullivan joined Core Scientific at thirty-two with a background in infrastructure M&A advisory; Nygaard arrived from the same Chicago boutique, XMS Capital Partners, in March 2025. The CEO-CFO pairing from a single middle-market investment bank is unusual in a company of Core Scientific's size and capital intensity. Transaction structuring — the CoreWeave contracts, the $3.3 billion project bond, the convertible note issuance — has been executed with evident sophistication. But running nine data center sites simultaneously, managing construction contractors across five states, and maintaining the operational discipline required to hit megawatt billing milestones is a different craft. Steve Smith's addition to the board in May 2026, drawing on his fifteen-year tenure as Equinix's CEO through that company's REIT conversion and global expansion, addresses the experience deficit in the boardroom. Whether comparable operational expertise exists inside Core Scientific's management team below the C-suite level is a question the public disclosures do not fully resolve.

## Risk 6: Regulatory and Power Market Exposure at Gigawatt Scale

Core Scientific's operational footprint spans Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, North Carolina, North Dakota, Texas, and Oklahoma — seven state regulatory jurisdictions with distinct utility commission frameworks, environmental review processes, and legislative appetites for data center oversight. The Pecos, Texas and Muskogee, Oklahoma development pipelines, each targeting 1.5 gigawatts of gross capacity, would make Core Scientific one of the largest single-site power consumers in their respective transmission zones.

FERC's interconnection queue reforms under Order 2023, effective since mid-2024, introduced a first-ready, first-served cluster study process designed to reduce speculative queue positions. The reforms improve long-term queue hygiene but have created near-term processing delays as grid operators work through accumulated backlogs. Core Scientific's existing interconnections are a competitive moat precisely because they pre-date those reforms; new greenfield interconnections at Pecos and Muskogee must navigate the reformed system.

State-level data center regulation is an emerging risk that did not exist in material form when the CoreWeave contracts were signed. Texas's 89th Legislature considered multiple bills in its 2025 session addressing data center water consumption, grid demand response obligations, and property tax treatment — reflecting growing political tension between the economic development benefits of large data center investments and their infrastructure demands. Oklahoma has been broadly welcoming of data center investment, but the scale of the Muskogee proposal — a 1.5-gigawatt development in a community of approximately 35,000 people — ensures that it will attract state-level policy attention regardless of initial receptiveness. Future federal carbon disclosure rules, if implemented with the scope originally contemplated by the SEC's climate disclosure framework, would add reporting obligations that are manageable in isolation but represent compliance cost and legal risk in a regulatory environment whose direction is uncertain.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Catalyst Calendar

The next twelve months open from a defined inflection point. In the first quarter of 2026, Core Scientific reported Adjusted EBITDA of positive $4.4 million — the first positive reading in the HPC transition era — on total revenue of $115.2 million, with colocation contributing $77.5 million as 243 megawatts billed to CoreWeave. The arithmetic of the forward ramp is mechanically simple: management guided for 450-plus megawatts billing by late summer 2026 and 590 megawatts by early 2027. Executing that ramp on schedule, across six construction sites simultaneously, against a $2 billion capital deployment program, is the operational question on which every material catalyst in the following twelve months resolves.

**Q2 2026** (results expected late July or early August 2026) is the first formal test of the capacity ramp. The 207-megawatt gap between Q1's 243-megawatt billing base and the late-summer target needs to be substantially closed in this period. The $3.3 billion project bond, priced in April 2026 at 7.75% and generating approximately $2.9 billion in net proceeds, funded construction reserves across the six CoreWeave sites; Q2 is the first full quarter in which contractors are operating against an unconstrained balance sheet. The quarter also brings the 2026 Annual Meeting, at which Chairman Jordan Levy departs the board — closing the governance reconstitution that began with the Two Seas Capital cooperation agreement in February. The identity of the director elected to the newly constituted chair role will be the first tangible signal of how aggressively the incoming board intends to operate independently of management.

**Q3 2026** (results expected late October or early November 2026) is the quarter in which 450 megawatts should be a confirmed billing figure rather than a guidance target. On the math from Q1's per-megawatt revenue rate, 450 megawatts billing implies quarterly colocation revenue in the $140–155 million range — annualizing at roughly $560–620 million, exceeding FY2025's entire company revenue of $319 million from colocation alone. The Two Seas cooperation agreement requires a second new independent director added by September 15, 2026; that addition represents the midpoint of a three-stage board reconstitution whose completion shapes the governance premium or discount applied to the stock. Mining consolidation should accelerate materially in Q3 as the converted capacity exits commissioning.

**Q4 2026** (results expected February 2027) should mark the practical completion of the legacy conversion program. Management stated the intention to consolidate self-mining to one or two sites by year-end 2026. If executed, Q4 will be the first quarter in which revenue mix is unambiguously dominated by long-term contracted colocation rather than bitcoin spot-price exposure. Construction milestones at Hunt County, Texas — the approximately 430-megawatt development announced in 2026 — and Port Muskogee Phase 1 (100 megawatts, under construction) will carry the forward narrative into 2027. The 590-megawatt early-2027 target implies a Q4 exit rate approaching that number.

**Q1 2027** (results expected April or May 2027) is the stated destination of the near-term roadmap: 590 megawatts billing, with annual colocation revenues running at approximately $750–800 million and gross margins at scale in the 80–85% guided range.

## Consensus Estimates

The per-megawatt colocation revenue implied by Q1 2026 actuals — $77.5 million across 243 megawatts — annualizes to roughly $1.28 million per megawatt. That figure sits below the long-term CoreWeave contract average implied by the $8.7 billion twelve-year agreement across approximately 390 megawatts (roughly $1.9 million per megawatt per year at maturity), reflecting phased commissioning and early-stage billing profiles at sites that came online late in the quarter. Per-megawatt yield should converge upward as sites exit ramp and enter steady-state operations.

| Period | Colo MW (est.) | Colo Revenue | Self-Mining Rev | Total Revenue | Adj. EBITDA Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2026A | 243 MW | $77.5M | ~$32M | $115.2M | ~4% |
| Q2 2026E | ~340–370 MW | ~$105–115M | ~$50–55M | ~$155–170M | ~18–22% |
| Q3 2026E | ~440–460 MW | ~$140–150M | ~$30–40M | ~$175–190M | ~32–38% |
| Q4 2026E | ~510–540 MW | ~$160–170M | ~$15–25M | ~$180–195M | ~42–48% |
| FY2026E | — | ~$480–510M | ~$160–175M | ~$640–690M | ~24–30% |
| FY2027E | ~590+ MW | ~$740–780M | ~$40–60M | ~$785–840M | ~50–58% |

*Estimates derived from Q1 2026 actuals, management capacity and margin guidance, and per-megawatt revenue run rates. FY2027 Adjusted EBITDA consensus of approximately $600–800 million is cited in sell-side coverage. Reported net income will continue to be dominated by non-cash items — warrant liability mark-to-market, stock-based compensation, and depreciation — making Adjusted EBITDA the operative comparator.*

On the guidance record, management's Q1 2026 commentary explicitly raised the margin target. The company moved the CoreWeave gross margin guide to 80–85%, up from the original 75–80%, citing operational efficiencies as sites exit commissioning and enter steady-state. For FY2026 capital expenditure, guidance of approximately $2 billion was affirmed, including the Hunt County site acquisition and the Polaris and Muskogee purchases.

## What to Watch Each Quarter

**Megawatts billing versus the guided ramp.** This is the single most important operational datapoint. Each megawatt of slippage represents approximately $1.3–1.9 million in annualized revenue at current per-megawatt yields. A quarter-end billing count even 40 megawatts below guidance implies a meaningful annualized revenue miss.

**Colocation gross margin trajectory.** The 80–85% guidance at scale is a structural claim — not a data center REIT margin (50–60% typical) but something closer to a pure-play contract infrastructure model. Any retreat toward 70% or below in a given quarter signals either pricing pressure from CoreWeave renegotiation, site-level operating cost overruns, or commissioning expenses flowing through the segment.

**Capital expenditure cadence versus the $2 billion full-year guide.** The project bond covers construction reserves; reimbursements from CoreWeave partially offset Core Scientific's outlays. Any mismatch between construction spend and reimbursement timing creates near-term cash flow pressure visible in the quarterly liquidity disclosures.

**Self-mining wind-down pace.** Management's one-to-two-site consolidation target by year-end 2026 is also a forward signal on HPC demand: a faster-than-guided wind-down implies conversion capacity is being absorbed by new colocation demand. A slower wind-down implies either stickier bitcoin economics or weaker HPC pipeline.

## Beat Versus Miss

A beat at Q2 2026 looks like: megawatts billing above 380 at quarter-end, colocation revenue above $115 million, colocation gross margins confirmed at or above 78%, and management guidance on the late-summer 450-megawatt target reaffirmed or raised. Any expansion of the CoreWeave contract scope — additional megawatts, extended terms, or pricing escalators — or announcement of a second named HPC tenant would constitute a material upside catalyst.

A miss looks like: megawatts billing below 320 at Q2 end, colocation gross margins below 72%, or any disclosure suggesting construction delay at a named CoreWeave site. A delay to the 450-megawatt ramp pushes revenue recognition into Q4, materially compressing FY2026 consensus. More severely, any signal of CoreWeave counterparty stress — payment deferral, force majeure invocation, or contract modification — would threaten the project bond coverage ratios and convert a growth narrative into a credit story. The project bond covenant structure, which was not fully disclosed as of the snapshot date, represents a latent disclosure risk.

## The Bull and Bear Asymmetry

The bull case is a valuation re-rating story at least as much as a revenue growth story. At the snapshot date, Core Scientific traded at a meaningful discount to the present value of its contracted revenue backlog — $8.7 billion from CoreWeave alone over twelve years — implying the market was applying a substantial discount for execution risk, customer concentration, and capital structure complexity. As megawatts ramp and gross margins reach guided levels, the blended company multiple should migrate from a mining-adjacent discount (~5–8x forward EBITDA) toward the data center operator range (~12–18x) that Equinix, Digital Realty, and their infrastructure peers command. A full re-rating, combined with FY2027 EBITDA consensus of $600–800 million, implies an equity value significantly above the $8 billion market capitalization at the snapshot date — before crediting any incremental HPC contracts beyond CoreWeave.

The bear case is more mechanical but structurally severe. The $3.3 billion project bond is senior secured against contracted cash flows. Execution slippage, CoreWeave financial stress, or a sustained bitcoin rally that makes mining megawatt reallocation economically irrational could each compress the revenue ramp that underwrites the debt service. With a stockholders' deficit of $962.7 million and no book-value backstop, the capital structure becomes the dominant narrative the moment the colocation growth story wobbles.

The distribution of outcomes is unusually wide. Core Scientific is, at this stage of its evolution, a construction company whose shares are priced as an AI infrastructure compounder. The next twelve months are the period in which those two descriptions either converge — or don't.

chapters.title: 2026–2030 Horizon: From Mining Legacy to Data Center Compounder
chapters.body:
## The 2026 Execution Agenda

When Adam Sullivan addressed investors after Core Scientific's first-quarter 2026 earnings release, the company had finally crossed a threshold that had taken two years of capital destruction to reach: positive Adjusted EBITDA of $4.4 million, with 243 megawatts actively billing to CoreWeave and $77.5 million in colocation revenue flowing through a single quarter. That one quarter's colocation revenue already exceeded the entire calendar year 2025 colocation line by a factor of nearly five. The trough was behind them. The question was how fast the climb continued.

The 2026 operational calendar carried four interlocking priorities. The first and most immediate was reaching 450-plus megawatts of billing capacity by late summer, the milestone management identified as the point at which colocation revenue alone would run ahead of total company revenue from any prior year. The second was commissioning Muskogee Phase 1 — the company's newest site at Port Muskogee, Oklahoma, where 100 megawatts of initial capacity was under construction within a longer 1.5-gigawatt gross development pipeline announced in November 2024. The third was completing the acquisition and beginning construction at Hunt County, Texas, where approximately 430 megawatts of gross capacity was being developed, with customer identity not yet publicly disclosed as of the snapshot. The fourth, and arguably most consequential for the long-term investor case, was initiating the permitting and transmission interconnection process for the 1.5-gigawatt Pecos development — a process that in the Texas grid typically requires two to four years from filing to energization and whose outcome would define the outer boundary of Core Scientific's growth trajectory into the next decade.

Concurrent with those greenfield and expansion programs, management guided for the consolidation of self-mining operations to one or two sites by year-end. Self-mining had generated $229.2 million of the company's $319.0 million in total FY2025 revenue — still the dominant segment numerically — but every megawatt redeployed to colocation represented a structural improvement in revenue quality, margin predictability, and capital efficiency. The arithmetic was unambiguous: a megawatt of mining capacity operating at bitcoin's prevailing economics generated perhaps $50,000 to $80,000 annually; the same megawatt under an HPC colocation contract at $8.7 billion across 390 megawatts over twelve years implied approximately $1.85 million per megawatt per year. The conversion imperative needed no further justification.

## A $700 Million Run Rate Takes Shape

The financial architecture of Core Scientific's 2027 state is largely deterministic once the contracted capacity schedule is accepted. CoreWeave's agreements, totaling approximately $8.7 billion in cumulative revenue over twelve-year terms across roughly 390 megawatts, imply an annualized run rate of approximately $725 million when fully billing — the figure the company's [Q1 2026 earnings materials](https://investors.corescientific.com/news-releases/news-release-details/core-scientific-reports-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) framed as the destination. With 590 megawatts targeted for billing by early 2027 — a figure that includes the additional $1.2 billion Denton expansion announced in February 2025 — the contracted annual revenue run rate on existing agreements approached the $700–750 million range by most analyst models, consistent with the research directive's implied mathematics.

| Metric | FY2025 Actual | Q1 2026 Annualized | FY2027 Estimate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Colocation Revenue | $65.4M | ~$310M | $700–750M |
| Total Revenue | $319.0M | ~$460M (blended) | $700–800M |
| Colocation Gross Margin | — | Guided 80–85% | 80–85% |
| Adjusted EBITDA | Negative | Inflecting | $600–800M (consensus) |

At 80 to 85 percent gross margins on the colocation contracts — a guidance range management raised from the original 75 to 80 percent in Q1 2026 — a $725 million revenue run rate would generate approximately $580 to $615 million in colocation gross profit. After corporate overhead, the company's consensus Adjusted EBITDA range of approximately $600 to $800 million for FY2027 represents the first year in which Core Scientific would begin to look, financially, less like a miner that pivoted and more like an infrastructure compounder.

## The Diversification Imperative: Beyond CoreWeave

The 1.5-gigawatt development pipelines at Pecos and Muskogee are the defining strategic question of the 2028–2030 period, and they carry a structural risk the contracted CoreWeave business does not: they are not yet sold. Building 3 gigawatts of gross power capacity — net leasable capacity likely 70 to 80 percent of that — without committed tenants would be among the largest speculative infrastructure bets in the sector. The capital investment required is enormous; the company's $3.3 billion [project bond in April 2026](https://investors.corescientific.com/news-releases/news-release-details/core-scientific-prices-33-billion-senior-secured-project-bonds) was sized for the already-contracted CoreWeave work, not for the greenfield pipelines.

The most likely tenant universe for those developments falls into two tiers. The first is CoreWeave itself, which would logically want to expand its contractual footprint as its own customer base grows; given the existing operational relationship, CoreWeave's demonstrated willingness to commit to twelve-year terms, and the financing validation the project bond provides, further CoreWeave expansion at Pecos or Muskogee carries the highest probability of any single counterparty. The second tier includes competing GPU cloud operators and hyperscalers. Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon — each running aggressive AI infrastructure programs — represent potential colocation customers at the scale of hundreds of megawatts, and Core Scientific's sites in the American South and Midwest offer transmission access, relatively low-cost power, and the operational track record of the CoreWeave deployments as a reference. No contracts with those parties were disclosed as of the snapshot date, but analyst coverage had routinely cited them as the most plausible expansion scenario.

Pricing dynamics in this segment were evolving rapidly. The CoreWeave twelve-year agreements — structured at roughly $1.85 million per megawatt annually — reflected 2024 market conditions, when AI infrastructure demand was outstripping supply by a significant margin. By 2027–2028, if hyperscaler-owned capacity and competing colo developers add meaningful gigawatts to the market, the price per megawatt for incremental contracts could compress. Core Scientific's competitive advantage in that environment rests on owned real estate and grid interconnections with irreplaceable lead times — not on price.

## The REIT Question

At sufficient billing scale — perhaps 1 to 2 gigawatts of contracted, stabilized capacity — Core Scientific's colocation business could theoretically satisfy the revenue and asset composition tests for Real Estate Investment Trust treatment. A REIT structure would require distributing at least 90 percent of taxable income to shareholders but would dramatically expand the investable universe: pension funds, insurance companies, and other yield-seeking institutional allocators that are structurally prohibited from owning growth-oriented C-corporations would become eligible buyers of Core Scientific equity. The multiple compression observed at Equinix and Digital Realty — trading at 18 to 22 times EV/EBITDA on the basis of dividend stability and institutional sponsorship — illustrates the potential cost-of-capital benefit.

Management had not publicly committed to a REIT pathway as of the snapshot. The appointment of Steve Smith — who as Equinix's chief executive from 2007 to 2018 oversaw that company's own REIT conversion and the buildout of its hyperscale interconnection model — to the Core Scientific board in May 2026 was read by several analysts as a signal that the question was at least being examined at the board level. The conditions for conversion are demanding: stabilized cash flows, resolution of the warrant liability overhang, simplification of the capital structure, and sufficient distributable income. None of those conditions were fully met at the snapshot date, but the trajectory pointed toward them.

## The Bitcoin Inheritance

Core Scientific retained a bitcoin treasury of $222 million at December 31, 2025 — a legacy of its self-mining operations and a recurring governance discussion as the self-mining segment winds down. The company's stated approach was neither to pursue an explicit accumulation strategy like Marathon Digital's ([MARA](https://investors.marathondh.com/)'s publicly declared policy of holding essentially all mined bitcoin as treasury) nor to liquidate systematically. Management had instead characterized the bitcoin holdings as a liquid asset available to fund capital needs, implying opportunistic rather than strategic treasury management.

The contrast with Marathon Digital is instructive. Marathon's explicit "hodl" posture has made its stock a leveraged proxy for bitcoin price — a characteristic that attracts a specific investor constituency and commands a bitcoin-premium valuation during bull markets but amplifies drawdowns. Core Scientific's trajectory was in the opposite direction: reducing bitcoin exposure as a proportion of enterprise value as contracted HPC revenue grows. The $222 million position, while meaningful, represented under 3 percent of the company's $8 billion market capitalization at the snapshot — a rounding error at scale, but a governance conversation that would return each time bitcoin prices moved materially.

## The Value Creation Thesis at Scale

The long-term investment case for Core Scientific depends on a simple but demanding proposition: that the company converts its development pipelines into contracted, billing capacity at economics similar to the CoreWeave agreements. If Pecos and Muskogee together reach 1.5 to 2 gigawatts of net leasable, fully contracted capacity by 2029–2030, the financial profile of the business changes by an order of magnitude.

At $1.85 million per megawatt annually — the implied CoreWeave rate — 1.5 gigawatts of billing capacity would generate approximately $2.8 billion in annual revenue; 2 gigawatts would generate approximately $3.7 billion. At 75 percent blended gross margins and reasonable operating cost assumptions, Adjusted EBITDA in the $2.0 to $2.8 billion range is a plausible scenario. Applied against data center operator multiples — Equinix has traded at 18 to 22 times EV/EBITDA — the implied enterprise value would be $36 to $62 billion, against a snapshot market capitalization of approximately $8 billion.

That arithmetic does not require optimism about pricing. It requires only execution — on permitting, interconnection, financing, and tenant relationships — at the scale and pace Core Scientific's management team has committed to publicly. The $3.3 billion project bond validated the bankability of the model at 390 megawatts. The question for the next five years is whether the operational and capital-markets machinery can replicate that validation three or four more times, in new states, with customers who are not yet named. At the snapshot date, the market was pricing that probability at a significant discount. Whether the discount proved warranted or prescient was the central question of the Core Scientific investment thesis.
