financials.key_finding:
Core Scientific presents one of the most striking revenue-profile discontinuities in the digital infrastructure sector: a company reporting $510.7 million in total revenue in FY2024 — while still operating primarily as a bitcoin miner — followed by $319.0 million in FY2025, a 37.5% decline that reflects the deliberate and capital-intensive destruction of its legacy mining revenue base in favor of a fundamentally different, higher-margin business. FY2025 was the trough year of the transition: self-mining contributed $229.2 million, colocation contributed just $65.4 million, and hosted mining added $24.4 million, while capital expenditure of $279.2 million (partially offset by $226.2 million in CoreWeave partnership reimbursements) was deployed to convert facilities.

The forward revenue trajectory is driven almost entirely by the scaling of the CoreWeave colocation contracts. As of Q1 2026, 243 megawatts were billing, contributing $77.5 million in colocation revenue in a single quarter — an annualized run rate of approximately $310 million from colocation alone, already exceeding all of FY2025 colocation revenue by 4.7 times in one quarter. With 450-plus megawatts targeted by late summer 2026 and 590 megawatts by early 2027, and with guidance for 80–85% gross margins on the CoreWeave contracts (up from the original 75–80% guide), the business is approaching a point where colocation revenue alone will exceed total company revenue of FY2025 before year-end 2026.

The capital structure is complex and event-driven. As of December 31, 2025, the company carried $1,060.3 million in 3.00% convertible notes due September 2029, a $936.1 million warrant liability (fair value, highly volatile), and a stockholders' deficit of $962.7 million. Cash and digital assets (bitcoin) totaled $533.4 million. The April 2026 $3.3 billion project bond at 7.75% due 2031 — net proceeds approximately $2.9 billion — fundamentally reshapes the balance sheet: existing debt was repaid and construction reserves funded across six CoreWeave sites. The project bond also crystallizes the financial logic of the colocation model: long-term, fixed-price contracts with a creditworthy counterparty support project finance at scale. With $2 billion in guided capital expenditure for 2026 alone (including approximately $700 million for the Hunt County site acquisition and the Polaris/Muskogee purchase), the company is in an aggressive growth investment phase that will pressure reported free cash flow while building contracted revenue backlog.
structural_observations: Revenue base is in active transition: FY2025 total revenue of $319.0M reflects trough-year transition dynamics, with self-mining ($229.2M) still dominant but colocation ($65.4M) on a steep growth trajectory; Q1 2026 colocation revenue of $77.5M already exceeds all of FY2025 colocation in a single quarter, pointing to rapid segment mix shift.

Fiscal year cadence is straightforward calendar-year (January–December), with quarterly earnings releases typically 30–45 days after quarter-end; the FY2024 financials were restated (no P&L/cash impact) due to improper capitalization of demolition-related asset values during the mining-to-colocation conversion, creating a minor disclosure risk flag for auditors.

Margin progression is the core financial narrative: colocation gross margins guided to 80–85% at scale (raised from original 75–80% guide in Q1 2026); FY2025 total gross profit was $37.9M on $319.0M revenue (11.9% blended margin), reflecting the drag of legacy mining; as colocation becomes dominant, blended gross margins are expected to approach the 70–80% range company-wide, implying a step-change in profitability that consensus FY2027 EBITDA estimates of approximately $600–800M capture.

Capital structure has three distinct layers: (1) $3.3B project bonds (7.75%, due 2031) — senior secured, backed by CoreWeave contract cash flows; (2) $1.06B convertible notes (3.00%, due Sep 2029, conversion rate ~90.93 shares per $1,000) — unsecured, equity-like at current share prices; (3) warrant liabilities ($936.1M fair value at Dec 31, 2025) — CORZW and CORZZ tranches issued in bankruptcy reorganization, creating large non-cash mark-to-market swings in reported net income each quarter.

Debt vs. equity dynamics: the company carries a stockholders' deficit of $962.7M as of Dec 31, 2025, driven by fresh-start accounting adjustments from the Chapter 11 emergence and accumulated non-cash losses; the true economic equity is the $8B market capitalization, reflecting the market's view of the present value of contracted and prospective colocation revenue streams; analysts value the stock primarily on EV/EBITDA against forward estimates rather than book value.

Comparable peers for valuation include: Riot Platforms (RIOT) — similar mining-to-AI pivot narrative, market cap ~$4–5B, at earlier stage; Marathon Digital (MARA) — primarily bitcoin treasury + mining, market cap ~$5–6B, minimal AI pivot; IREN (Iris Energy) — AI/HPC pivot, smaller scale; Equinix (EQIX) — data center REIT, the aspirational peer for colocation multiple (~20x EV/EBITDA); Digital Realty (DLR) — another REIT comp; the key valuation question is whether CORZ ultimately commands a mining-company multiple (~5–8x) or a data center operator multiple (~15–20x) as the revenue mix shifts.

Market cap volatility is extreme: 52-week range of $10.46–$26.83 as of the snapshot date, with a beta of 5.45; the stock is highly sensitive to bitcoin price, CoreWeave news flow, power capacity announcements, and AI infrastructure sentiment broadly; the failed CoreWeave acquisition, the Two Seas activist campaign, and the $3.3B project bond each drove multi-day moves of 20–40%, making CORZ one of the most event-driven large-cap infrastructure names in the market.

leadership.key_finding:
Core Scientific's leadership team is notable for being largely installed during or immediately after the Chapter 11 proceeding, giving the company an unusual characteristic: its executives are architects of the current strategy rather than inheritors of the failed one. CEO Adam Sullivan, age 33 at the snapshot date, was recruited from XMS Capital Partners in May 2023 while the company was still in bankruptcy, with the explicit mandate to execute the HPC pivot. Sullivan's background is investment banking — specifically digital-asset and infrastructure M&A — not operations, a profile that explains both the sophistication of the CoreWeave transaction structuring and some of the execution complexity that has emerged as construction management at billion-dollar scale differs from transaction advisory. CFO James Nygaard, age 50, joined in March 2025 from the same firm — XMS Capital, where he was Sullivan's colleague for six years as Head of M&A. The CEO-CFO partnership from a single boutique investment bank is unusual in a company of Core Scientific's size and has attracted governance commentary; it also means both executives share a transaction-centric worldview that may underweight the operational complexity of running nine data center sites simultaneously.

The board underwent substantial reconstitution through 2025–2026. The Two Seas Capital cooperation agreement (February 2026) effectively acknowledged that the incumbent board — assembled at the January 2024 emergence — was not adequately independent of management for the scale of capital decisions the company faces. The addition of Steve Smith (former Equinix CEO, current Zayo Group CEO) in May 2026 brings the single most directly relevant data center operational credential to the boardroom; his fifteen years leading Equinix through its REIT conversion and international expansion represent exactly the institutional knowledge Core Scientific needs as it scales from mining operator to data center landlord. No private equity sponsor holds a controlling position; the company is genuinely public with a dispersed shareholder base of institutional and retail investors, with Two Seas Capital as the most visible organized minority bloc at approximately 9.9% (capped by standstill).
research_notes_for_writer: Dig into the XMS Capital Partners partnership: both CEO Sullivan and CFO Nygaard came from the same small Chicago boutique; XMS was the advisor on multiple billion-dollar bitcoin mining infrastructure transactions; the chapter writer should explore whether any XMS-advised transactions prior to Core Scientific's SPAC merger involved the same counterparties or equipment lenders whose debt was converted to equity in the restructuring — relevant for any related-party or conflict-of-interest analysis.

Adam Sullivan's age (33) and compensation ($22.92M, 96.4% in equity/bonuses) relative to the company's size and stage deserve treatment: he is one of the youngest CEOs of a multi-billion-dollar Nasdaq-listed infrastructure company; his ownership stake (~0.72%, ~$57.4M) creates meaningful alignment but also raises the question of what his dilution path looks like as the company issues equity for acquisitions and conversions.

The failed CoreWeave acquisition is a governance case study: the board initially approved the all-stock deal in July 2025; Two Seas Capital organized opposition; shareholders voted ~10:1 against in October 2025; this sequence raises questions about whether the board adequately represented shareholder interests in evaluating the deal, what the financial advisors' fairness opinions said, and how the company's independence narrative is now framed against the backdrop of having a customer (CoreWeave) that attempted to acquire it.

Jordan Levy's departure as Chairman (announced February 2026; not standing for re-election at 2026 annual meeting) removes the key connection to the post-bankruptcy creditor base — Levy came from SBNY and had relationships with the noteholders who became equity holders in the restructuring; the writer should examine who, if anyone, now represents that original post-reorganization shareholder constituency.

Steve Smith's addition as a director (May 2026) warrants deep biographical treatment: as CEO of Equinix from 2007 to 2018, he oversaw the company's REIT conversion, its expansion to 200-plus data centers globally, and the buildout of the hyperscale interconnection model; his perspective on whether Core Scientific's colocation model is genuinely comparable to mature colo operators or is a transitional structure should be sought in any public remarks.

Russell Cann (Chief Development Officer, 9.3 years tenure) is the longest-serving executive, having survived both the SPAC era and the bankruptcy; his institutional knowledge of site selection, permitting, and grid interconnection across the company's nine-plus operational sites is irreplaceable; the chapter writer should assess why he has stayed and what his role is in the current expansion programs at Pecos, Muskogee, and Hunt County.

The company's proxy statement (DEF 14A) filings on SEC EDGAR contain director compensation tables, stock ownership charts, and related-party transaction disclosures that should be reviewed for any governance flags not visible in press releases — particularly any relationships between board members and CoreWeave, NVIDIA, or infrastructure equity sponsors.
